editorials.title: Treat Himalayas as one disaster zone, coordinate data to improve response
editorials.passage: Wednesday's furious flash floods and landslides on the Nepal-Tibet border show how closely interconnected the Himalayan region is as an ecological disaster zone. An extreme event in the mountains can affect communities far away, across national borders. What happens in one part of the Himalayas cannot be regarded as any one country’s problem. The danger extends across the region.For India, the concern is immediate and geographical. The Tibetan-origin Lhende river, where the flooding initiated, forms the Bhote Koshi in Nepal, which flows downstream as the Trishuli and the Narayani, which flows farther into India as the Gandak. What happens in the upper reaches of the river system can affect people downstream. The Himalayan rivers make cooperation on disasters a practical necessity, whatever the political circumstances.The latest floods also point to a changing pattern of Himalayan risk. No rain fell when flooding occurred. The trigger appears to have been a glacier collapse and an ice-rock avalanche, followed by a temporary blockage and the sudden release of water and debris. This differs from the familiar picture of flooding and shows why disaster warnings in the mountains have to look beyond rainfall.Weather forecasts will need to be backed by closer monitoring of glaciers, unstable slopes and other sources of sudden flooding. In the mountains, such events can develop rapidly, leaving little time to evacuate. Climate change must be part of this discussion, with continuously evaluated evidence. The broader changes in the Himalayas are clear. The region is warming and its glaciers are rapidly losing ice. These changes make it important to understand how risks are evolving rather than assume that past patterns will always hold..Infrastructure presents another challenge. Roads, bridges, hydropower and tourism facilities are necessary for Himalayan communities and their economies. But projects in the mountains must account carefully for unstable slopes, glacial lakes, changing river flows and the risk of sudden landslides and floods.India can play an important role in strengthening cooperation with Nepal and, where possible, China. A Himalayan disaster compact could provide for sharing satellite and river data, joint monitoring of vulnerable areas, better early-warning systems and closer coordination during rescue and evacuation. The priority should be to build systems that allow countries to anticipate risks, share information quickly and respond together when disasters strike..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Hijab-clad girls puncture patriarchy in Onam dance
editorials.passage: A video clip of hijab-clad students celebrating Onam in a high school in Kerala’s Malappuram district, where Muslims make up more than two-thirds of the population, has drawn widespread appreciation online. Wearing traditional Kasavu-themed attires along with matching hijabs, these girls were recorded dancing with their schoolmates during celebrations held at their institutions. The video stood out among the thousands of similar ones that flooded social media over the past few days by showing that religion was no bar when it came to embracing the festival’s inclusive spirit with zest. The dance acquired added significance because these young Muslim girls were braving the diktats of orthodox religious scholars who had warned against partaking in the festivities. Such fatwas were issued during the past few Onams, too. But a number of young Muslim girls defied them this time to dance along unapologetically. Some girls even posted on social media asking the clerics to explain the rationale behind banning them from participating in Onam.It is indeed curious that the clerics who were offended by girls’ participation in the festivities were silent on Muslim boys taking part. It exposes the fact that religion is not the real issue here, but the patriarchy of clergymen who could not digest the fact that girls were no longer confined within the circle they had drawn. Such diktats, when openly defied, only serve to weaken their standing within the community even as they try to accentuate divisive feelings during a joyous occasion. Sensible voices within the community should restrain the clerics from making remarks that leave a negative imprint on society as a whole. It was a harmonious gesture of Panakkad Sayyid Sadik Ali Shihab Thangal, state president of Indian Union Muslim League and one of the most respected figures among Muslims in Kerala, to take part in the celebrations..As these young girls wearing traditional costumes danced their way to glory, the secular psyche of Kerala clapped in approval. Women from all communities keep breaking glass ceilings and finding their own space in all walks of life. They should not be restrained with patriarchal decrees that intend to curb their freedom. As these young girls showed, perhaps the best way to smash patriarchy is to dance on it..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | A jeweller's eye
editorials.passage: Ebrahim Alkazi, who expanded the vocabulary and visuals of theatre, also had a keen eye for images old and new. His vision for preserving the old can be seen in his carefully-maintained archive of some of the earliest photographs of India, now curated by his grandson Rahaab Allana. Along with his wife Roshen, Alkazi also supported modernist women artists. Among them was Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese pop art pioneer who did to polka dots what Pablo Neruda saw spring doing to the cherry trees. The Center for International Contemporary Arts, which Alkazi founded in New York, revived Kusama’s career in 1989 with a solo show that thrust her unapologetic art and self into the global imagination. Her recent passing reminds us that, in the world of art, it takes one to know one..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Code of conduct
editorials.passage:
At least once a year, one particular Hindu text — the Manusmriti — resurfaces in the political discourse, leading to an uproar. The Manusmriti is part of a collection of treatises known as the dharmashastras that discuss socio-structural, legal and ethical norms. Among all the dharmashastras , the Manusmriti became an important document because of the number of times it has been referred to in subsequent writings. There are more commentaries on the Manusmriti than on any of the other dharmashastras . Apart from being a dominant text in this genre through medieval India, its influence also extended to Buddhist Southeast Asia. Long before William Jones translated the Manusmriti , it was a pre-eminent text on dharma . Its 20th-century political significance comes from Babasaheb Ambedkar’s attack on the text and its discriminative social prescriptions.

Whenever the disturbing nature of the Manusmriti ’s contents is brought up, the following defence is provided: ‘How many people have even read it?’ Or ‘Hindus don’t know anything about the Manusmriti . Neither do they follow its dictums.’ The argument is that the Manusmriti is irrelevant to Hindu social practices because it is not widely read, nor has it been shared among the larger Hindu community. The assertion that a text needs to be read to become part of public practice is fallacious. If serious reading is the basis of practice, then one can argue that the Vedas themselves have no practical socio-religious relevance. The number of people who could learn or understand Vedic Sanskrit was always limited by caste. Exceptions were few and far between. The common people have very little idea of what it actually says. Even in the 21st century, the majority of those who interpret the Vedas come from the Brahmanical castes. Yet, a large section of Hindus revere the Vedas because they have been told to do so by generations of Brahmins who have controlled Vedic knowledge.

When Prime Minister Narendra Modi repeatedly uses the phrase, “ Ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti ” (the truth is one, the learned call it by many names), from the Rig Veda as an example of ‘our’ civilisational culture, who does he include in the ‘we’? Does he include all Indians or just a select few? If one is to accept that the essence of that expression is imbibed by the majority through stories and practices, then it needs to be acknowledged that written texts find their way into social and religious practices without society at large even having read its contents. In other words, the Manusmriti being socially operative has little to do with the knowledge of its actual words.

Even those who argue that the Manusmriti is not a primary text quote from it when it is convenient! When the then deputy chief minister of Tamil Nadu, Udhayanidhi Stalin, triggered political outrage with his remarks on sanatan dharma , a quote from the Manusmriti was used to explain its meaning. The translation of the verse reads as follows: ‘He should say what is true, and he should say what is pleasant; he should not say what is true but unpleasant, and he should not say what is pleasant but untrue — that is the eternal dharma .’

This is considered samanya dharma or that which is common to all people regardless of varna , gender, or age. But this very treatise also directly discriminates against others on the basis of dharma . Dharma has multiple meanings and, depending on the context, it can turn from an embracing quality to a parochial social duty or enforced obligation. Therefore, you cannot cherry-pick a verse that suits a narrative.

The Manusmriti lives on because casteist and misogynistic practices that mirror its words are everyday realities in India. The manner in which the Dalits are treated, the segregation of water wells, the denial of common cremation grounds, honour killings, domestic violence against women, and the objectification of women in our cinemas emanate directly from the Manusmriti playbook. Discriminative social practices always morph and adapt to changing times. Direct physical violence transforms into psychological and emotional violence and subtler forms of discrimination and denials. The fact that there is a protest against reservations is proof of manuvad thinking. Listening to the thoughts of a few of these protesters was shocking, to say the least. A statue of Manu welcomes you into the Rajasthan High Court in Jaipur, and continues to do so despite many demands for its removal. A number of high court judges have also referred to the Manusmriti . Only recently, a purification ceremony was conducted because the president of the Indian National Congress, Mallikarjun Kharge, who belongs to the Dalit community, had addressed a gathering in Haldwani, Uttarakhand. Manu is far from dead.

Manuvad is also alive within progressive savarnas . The so-called enlightened ones often deny their own participation in casteism and patriarchy. How many times have we heard savarnas speak with pride and eloquence about their upbringing being caste-less, name friends from ‘other castes’, or throw in anecdotes about how they treated their house helps? They seem oblivious to the fact that caste has designed each of these social interactions. Invisible in their narrations are the individuals whom they are speaking about. Caste even allows a savarna to feel empowered by the smallest acts of kindness. Being caste blind is not anti-caste.

Criticism of the Manusmriti or any Hindu text brings out pushback that is primarily whataboutery. What about Islam? There is no doubt that prejudice and Othering are embedded in Islam or, for that matter, in all religions. It is essential that people from within those religious locations address these markers. There are many Islamic scholars and activists who have been pushing for reform within Islam. Instead of standing with them as allies, we use their words to further demonise Muslims and Islam. The triple talaq verdict came about because five brave Muslim women took the lead. Yet, the credit for the judgment has been appropriated by Modi and the Bharatiya Janata Party.

We have also fallen for the often-heard proclamation that Hinduism is diverse but comes together in the expression ‘ aham brahmasmi ’ (I am brahman ). The inference is that this eliminates discrimination. This is untrue. Also, such a universal explanation needs temperance. Philosophical discussions about the self and the divine are more often than not viewed only from the advaitic lens, deeply influenced by figures such as Vivekananda. It has been forgotten that even within Brahmanical traditions, there are two major philosophical streams: vishishtadvaita and advaita . The same verses from the Upanishads have different interpretations in these philosophies. Other philosophical modes that emanated from other sections of society also demand attention. All these ideas are in constant contestation with one another. Despite these innumerable philosophical moorings, most Hindus have a transactional relationship with their gods. Rituals are all about appeasing the deities, removing obstacles, fear and so on. Similarly spiritual-humanistic expositions do not demolish the ugliness in human interactions.

If there is one text that brings Hindu diversity together, it is, ironically, the Manusmriti . A social explanator that keeps Hindu society within its order, surreptitiously modifying itself to suit the times. Which is why Ambedkar burnt it.

T.M. Krishna is a leading Indian musician and a prominent public intellectual

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: The row over Kriti Sanon's Raksha Bandhan advertisement exposes a warped mindset
editorials.passage:
Sir — Policing women’s clothes is not exactly new in New India. A jewellery brand’s Raksha Bandhan advertisement featuring Kriti Sanon was recently withdrawn after controversy over the actor’s outfit. Kangana Ranaut — she has many admirers in the saffron brigade — called out Sanon for tying rakhi in what she described as a “bikini”, implying that such an outfit in front of one’s brother is at odds with Indian culture. To think a woman dressing stylishly in front of her brother is an act of provocation reveals a warped mindset. It is 2026 and, yet, women’s bodies continue to be treated as a cultural battleground.

Shrestha Majumder, Calcutta

Sir — This is in reference to the article, “Inclusion: 7 Lakh, Purge: 31 Lakh”, published on August 26 in The Telegraph . I am directed to state that the Office of the Chief Electoral Officer has not supplied any such information under RTI Act to any query whatsoever as specified in the opening sentence of the news.

Additional Chief Electoral Officer, West Bengal

The Telegraph responds: The Additional Chief Electoral Officer, West Bengal has clarified that the Office of the Chief Electoral Officer “has not supplied any such information under RTI Act to any query whatsoever as specified in the opening sentence of the news”. He was referring to the intro of the paper’s lead story which stated, “The Supreme Court was on Tuesday informed that only 7 lakh of the 38 lakh appeals before the SIR tribunals in Bengal were related to deletions from the voter list while the remaining 31 lakh were pleas challenging inclusions.”

The report was based on both the oral and written submissions made by the senior advocate, Gopal Sankaranarayanan, and the advocate-on-record, Neha Rathi, before a bench comprising the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana. The submissions were widely reported across all major national news dailies, legal portals, websites and television channels.

Responding to the clarifications, Neha Rathi told The Telegraph that the submissions were made as part of the pleadings and averments filed on behalf of the petitioner, the West Bengal Pradesh Congress Committee SIR Cell chairperson, Prosenjit Bose, for whom they both appeared.

Rathi stated that the said submissions were made mainly based on an article dated 06.08.2026 that was published in The Telegraph Online titled “Only 7 lakh of deleted 27 lakh have appealed before SIR tribunals in Bengal: Official”. The said news report was placed before the Supreme Court by the petitioner and their counsels by way of annexure (AI page 16-17) documents of 64-page Interim Application. She asked, “Why did they not object when The Telegraph first reported it on August 6?”

The counsel further said that the oral submissions were also made on the basis of RTI information received by “Isha Khan Choudhury, Member of Parliament from Dakshin Malda, Kotwali P-5 English Bazar, Malda” which were also placed before the Supreme Court for consideration.

Based on the submissions, the Hon’ble Supreme Court was pleased to pass an order seeking various information from the ECI represented by the senior advocate, D. Sheshadri Naidu.

Sir — Unified Payments Interface completed 10 years on August 25. It is perhaps time to pause and assess its present utility and consider its future implications. Its most striking achievement has been its simplicity. Money transfers, once associated with account numbers, banking procedures, waiting and inconvenience, became seamless and hassle-free. UPI’s benefits have also crossed India’s borders, expanding to Sri Lanka, Singapore, Bhutan, Mauritius, France and other countries.

Yet, the very simplicity and the scale that make UPI transformative have created a new vulnerability. Cyber fraud has cast a shadow on the digital-payment revolution. Phishing links, fraudulent QR codes, impersonation, fake customer-care calls, and deceptive payment requests exploit technological weaknesses and moments of human trust or inattention.

Vijay Singh Adhikari, Nainital

Sir — Extending financial services beyond the physical realm into the digital one has been made possible by the UPI system. UPI continues to transform India’s digital payment ecosystem. The financial autonomy enabled by UPI has also brought more citizens into the formal financial system, making it more accessible and inclusive.

Sir — The Karnataka government recently passed the Karnataka Government Parks (Preservation) (Amendment) Bill, 2026, paving the way for alienation of up to 5% of the total area of a park or garden for public utility projects. This is clearly a volte-face on the Green Bengaluru initiative. Handing over park and garden land for development projects will damage these spaces, mar their beauty and undermine their ecology. Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar seems to be yielding to the real-estate lobby to raise funds for his cash-strapped party.

editorials.title: Tongue tamed
editorials.passage:
“My tongue will tell the anger of my heart,” Katherina had defiantly declared in The Taming of the Shrew . Yet, over four centuries later, a woman expressing her anger still causes “cultural shock” — and not just to the prime minister of India. None can miss the irony of people being simultaneously unsettled by women who use cuss words while comfortably rattling off abuses that invoke mothers and sisters or refer to female genitalia and prostitution. Abusing women and their bodies thus becomes the means of expressing male hostility, even camaraderie, but the women themselves are expected to remain politely silent.

However, language has always been biased against women. In Mother Tongue: The Surprising History of Women’s Words , Jenni Nuttall follows the English vocabulary used for female bodies and experiences across more than a thousand years, revealing that language divides women into acceptable and unacceptable kinds, prescribes how they should behave, and limits what they may say about themselves.

The word, woman, itself has become misleading in its modern iteration. It comes from the Old English wifman , meaning a female human; wif had nothing to do with being a wife as it is now understood, fusing the very existence of a ‘woman’ to her husband. ‘Girl’ once referred to a young person of any sex, but gradually became female and is now seen as an inferior state of being — ‘overtly’ emotional men are often chastised as being akin to ‘little girls’. Other names, too, have come to sort women according to their relationships with men. Mistress once meant a woman with authority before becoming a married man’s lover. Spinster, which began as an occupational term for a woman who spun thread, became a legal description of an unmarried woman, even a social insult for failing to secure a husband.

Language grows especially harsh when women depart from approved sexual conduct: take sl*t, wh*re and harl*t, for instance. Sl*t carried associations of dirt and slush before coming to denote promiscuity because evidently only the woman is rendered dirty when she chooses what to do with her body. Harl*t once described rogues of any kind, then settled almost exclusively upon women, and wh*re meant a person who desires. Female desire became grimy while male desire remained legitimate, if not chivalrous.

The taming also reached the body. In The Miller’s Tale , Chaucer wrote freely of the woman’s nether regions as perfectly regular anatomical parts. Yet, medical vocabulary that came years after him was uncomfortable describing a woman’s body. Pudendum , a term for the external female genitals, comes from a Latin root meaning shame. Hysteria came from the Greek word for womb and turned into a false theory about female anatomy and then a diagnosis of female irrational­ity. Frigid once described sex­ually incapable men but by the 20th century, it had become an accusation against women who displayed too little sexual desire.

Words to describe how women speak followed the same disparaging pattern. An assertive man is attractive but an assertive woman is overstepping her place, being bossy or a shrew. Similarly, a cussing woman refuses the patriarchal demand for verbal pleasantness. This is important because swear words can express pain, anger, intimacy, humour and solidarity. Laboratory experiments have even found that profanity has communicative and physiological functions: repeating a swear word can increase pain tolerance. Women lose access to such cathartic functions of cussing when their speech is judged through an extra code of respectability. Casteist, communal and misogynistic slurs retain their violence regardless of the speaker’s sex. But the real ‘cultural shock’ perhaps is women reclaiming the right to speak what is on their minds.

editorials.title: Tricky terrain: Editorial on the multiple challenges to progress in India-China border talks
editorials.passage:
India and China have signalled progress in their border talks after a meeting between the national security adviser, Ajit Doval, and the Chinese foreign minister, Wang Yi, indicating that they might move towards delimiting some points along their contested boundary. The talks between Mr Doval and Mr Wang and the optimism reflected in the statements issued by New Delhi and Beijing are welcome. However, any real progress faces multiple challenges — both political and practical. And India must stay careful of both domestic political traps and diplomatic tensions as it tries to navigate what is the most consequential relationship in the neighbourhood. As the Indian government has consistently argued, the health of that relationship depends on peace along the border. That must remain the red line for India. Recent reports from Arunachal Pradesh suggesting that Chinese activities have forced Indian forces to abandon some patrol posts serve as a reminder of the perils of New Delhi taking its eye off the ball in ties with Beijing, even briefly. China, after all, has a track record of constantly testing its neighbours with pinpricks — with India along their long border, and with its Southeast Asian and East Asian neighbours in the high seas.

Yet that record, including incursions by Chinese forces on the eve of important bilateral meetings, must not by themselves deter India from pursuing diplomacy. What they must do is underscore for Indian negotiators the need to stay clear-eyed in talks with Beijing. Despite the positive tone of the statements issued by both countries, many parts of the so-called Line of Actual Control between India and China remain contested: New Delhi and Beijing disagree over not only what their final border should look like but also which parts they each control in reality. Agreeing to any delimitation will not be easy. For any Indian government, domestic perceptions are also important. Narendra Modi’s government has still not fully explained whether Chinese forces have occupied territory previously controlled by Indian forces in Ladakh after their altercation a few years ago in the region. What the government needs is to stay transparent with the people; what the Opposition needs to avoid is narrow politics over a matter of national security. But the government must shun the temptation of conceding any ground ahead of the upcoming BRICS summit for which it hopes to host the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The border is tricky terrain. India must tread with care.

editorials.title: Washed away: Editorial on the growing threat of glacial floods in the Himalayas
editorials.passage:
The disaster that has befallen Nepal and Tibet is being felt all around the world. Over 350 people are dead — the toll is feared to rise — in Nepal and many more are missing after a flash flood originating in neighbouring Tibet pulverised central Nepal on Wednesday. The death toll in Tibet is expected to be substantial as well. Worse, the danger is not over. There is concern that the rising lake waters may lead to a second flood. Citizens from a number of countries have lost their lives: hence the global impact of the tragedy. Nepal’s breathtaking natural beauty and its importance as a religious and spiritual site make the country a hub of tourists, many of whom have now perished or are unaccounted for. Indians form the largest share of the dead; several are missing, including residents of Calcutta, adding to the anxiety of their families. The Narendra Modi government has been fleet-footed in its response and has committed support and humanitarian assistance. There are worries on the domestic front as well, given that Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh are located downstream from Nepal. An interconnected river system in spate does not obey borders.

Glacial events — often the trigger for such mayhem — are of many types and are by no means novel in this part of the world. Sikkim had suffered a glacial lake outburst flood three years ago, as did Chamoli in 2021. In this episode, it had been assumed, initially, that an earthquake in Tibet was the likely cause of the frightful chain of events. But the United States Geological Survey has confirmed subsequently that a glacial collapse, resulting in a flash flood and debris flow, led to the catastrophe. This should draw attention to the risks confronting the region that falls within in the Himalayan arc since many glacial lakes are located across this stretch. Greater investments need to be made when it comes to tracking glacial lakes and installing early warning mechanisms. Could a transnational template be conceived of involving the cooperation of adversely affected nations? Land use patterns inimical to the local ecology need to change. Perhaps the biggest challenge would be to minimise ‘development’ work in the fragile Himalayan region given the geostrategic imperatives. But as climate change intensifies, such disasters are only expected to become more frequent. Rogue development construction activities cannot be the way forward.

editorials.title: Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love
editorials.passage:
D onald Trump has framed his theme for the midterm elections. It has come to him as naturally and inevitably as staring into the mirror, beyond any logic or argument, his definitive answer to no specific issue, providing no understanding of any particular problem, but transcending all of them. His political theme is more primal than programmatic, more instinctive than analytical, a heartfelt expression to protect his greatest romantic attachment, his obsessive fixation, his idealized object: himself.

Trump’s campaign theme is unrequited love. Unlike the pollsters, media consultants and pundits, he alone has grasped the magnitude and the source of the existential crisis threatening his politics. He has identified the problem for the Republicans as the faltering measure of complete devotion to him. His demand has nothing to do with mutual affection. It is a ploy to reassert his slipping control, a manipulative test to prove loyalty to him, or else. There can be no absolute rule without an absolute ruler; no absolute ruler without absolute submission; no absolute submission without the expression of absolute love. His sadness at its fading gives way to anger, paranoia and greater acts of retribution. He equates the fear he instills as a form of love. Trump accepts subservience, from whatever motive, as affection or its closest equivalent. He cares nothing about sincerity, so it’s all in the show. The less love displayed, the more fear required. Yet there is no rebound, but only deeper rejection.

Trump is heading toward the floor for presidential unpopularity – Nixon during Watergate on the eve of his resignation, Truman late in his second term at the depth of the Korean war, and George W Bush at the 2008 financial crash . But Trump’s breakdown differs uniquely from theirs. His decline has come earlier in his term, been more sustained, and his disintegration has not stabilized but is accelerating. He is being crushed by the accumulation of catastrophic events of his own making to which his impulsive response is to double down in each and every area. Stalemated in his reckless Iran war, he has now launched a heedless trade war against Canada that will devastate Republican candidates in the northern tier of states. His latest vanity project is gestural retribution to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, a watery ballroom. Admission of error for Trump would be the denial of self-love.

Trump began his campaign on his unrequited love theme on 16 August during a Fox News interview in which he discussed his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, leaving her job after just having a baby. He had held her up as meeting his highest criterion in remarks last December: “Isn’t she great? Is Karoline great? … She gets up there with that beautiful face and those lips that don’t stop, ba ba ba like a little machine gun.” Now, he tried to make a joke of her departure that expressed resentment at abandonment. “In fact, she likes her children more than she likes Trump. I’m very concerned about that,” he said. Then he repeated his unfunny “joke” at a campaign rally in South Carolina on 21 August: “I just learned she loves the baby more than she loves Donald Trump, and I’m very angry …” Trump’s lame attempt at humor was a rare instance of his truth-telling and self-revelation, a contemporary illustration of Freud’s Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious.

Trump was in South Carolina to campaign for his chosen candidate in the Republican primary, Darline Graham, who he had insisted be appointed to the Senate seat of her brother Lindsey Graham after he died on 11 July. Darline Graham confessed to cluelessness when asked in a debate about her position on Taiwan. “National security is not my thing,” she answered . “I’m not … that informed on national security.” But she was fully informed on the necessity of obedience to Trump. “You saved our country, and I want to thank you for that,” she said at the rally. Trump praised his worshipper: “She’s got a good gene pool.” She was born to love him. She stood in stark contrast to the immigrants he had described as “poisoning the blood of our country”.

Then Trump called on the crowd to embrace his new theme. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot … So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time. You got to say it.” He wishes every candidate to sound like Darline Graham in proclaiming him the national savior. He insists he is beloved, and if those who revere him turn out the Republicans must win. In fact, though he is not on the ballot in the midterm elections, Trump is the central issue. Voters do not have to “pretend, please”.

Trump intuitively comprehends that the midterm elections are about him in a way that makes this midterm unlike any other. In the marrow of his bones, he senses it is a crisis of his cult of personality.

Trump’s Maga was never a new party structure, but constructed on his wreckage of the old Republican party. In its place, every particle of the replacement is connected to the leader to advance his supremacy and self-enrichment. Everything flows upward, all heads tilted, all knees bent. Maga has always been Maga Inc of, by and for one man. The movement is the man.

When charisma fails, the movement implodes. If the leader is not worshipped, his uber-principle – the leader principle – collapses: no fuhrerprinzip , no Führer.

Trump’s plea for their unconditional love – “pretend, please” – defies gravity. He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails. Intensity is gauged by “strongly approve” and “strongly disapprove” poll numbers. More than the general statistics of approval or disapproval, these provide insight into the motivation of voters that determine the contour of elections. Trump now stands at 13% “strongly approve” in the most recent Reuters-Ipsos Poll . His “strongly disapprove” rating is at 49%. His total approval is at 33%, while disapproval is at 65%. Those in the “somewhat approve” category include low propensity soft voters especially inclined to skip midterm elections. And this poll was taken before his declaration of trade war against Canada.

All along, the Republicans have been Trump’s indispensable accomplices. Even if they were disposed to object, they could do nothing to draw him back from his “pretend, please” campaign. His anxiety to rescue his invincible image from the reality he’s created makes him more inescapable than ever. Any effort to restrict him will provoke his rage. He will not diminish himself for the sake of the party or even his own future. He plans to spend millions from his Maga Inc political action committee to tell the voters that they have never had it so good – “the greatest economy we’ve ever had, by far”, he says . He has mocked the suggestion that “affordability” might be a problem for many – it’s “a word they”, the media, “devised”, he has said . Trump intends to stage a mini convention in Dallas on 9 September, featuring Donald Trump to “celebrate … our achievements”. Republicans are locked almost uniformly into blind support, with the Maine senator Susan Collins venturing hollow criticism of the Canadian tariffs that makes her seem powerless and infuriates the remaining Maga base. Just as Trump has trapped himself, he has trapped the Republicans. The expenditure of tens of millions to depict his dire consequences as paradise on earth will have the unintended effect of supercharging the already motivated “strongly disapprove” voters and disillusion those who cannot help but be aware of the actual conditions of their own lives.

The sudden surfacing of Natalie Harp as a meme at this particular moment propitiously coincides with the wobbling of Trump’s cult. The 35-year-old is his model of the perfect staffer, perfect companion and perfect American citizen. If unrequited love is the problem, she is the solution. In Trump’s hierarchy of need, his pyramid of status, love and self-actualization, she is at the apex.

Harp is his “binky”, as Maggie Haberman of the New York Times has called her, his comfort blanket, his plush bunny rabbit. The “human printer” who trails after him, pressing the button to churn out an endless stream of adulatory articles, conspiracy theories and “alternative facts”, has become an extension of his nervous system. The former anchor at the fringe far-right One America News Network serves as Trump’s personal anchor. Harp broadcasts around the clock to an audience of one. She is the connector to the neurons of the far right, serving as a conduit to dodgy characters such as Laura Loomer with her lists of national security officials who were supposedly disloyal. Harp is Trump’s neurotransmitter who distributes a steady supply of dopamine and delusion.

Harp’s self-abasing devotion to Trump, expressed in her letters to him, serves as a kind of inadvertent political manifesto for the cult, a template for followers. Harp tellingly muddles a line from Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice – Mr Bennet blessing his strong-willed daughter Elizabeth in her engagement to Darcy – to demean herself and offer subservience to Trump: “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ – And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” In another letter, after self-disparaging apologies, Harp writes: “You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life … With all my Heart.”

As public opinion curdles on Trump, no longer able to “pretend, please”, Harp has not come to the wisdom of Conway Twitty in his 1959 rockabilly hit :

My only prayer will be Someday you’ll care for me But it’s only make believe

Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man , Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth . He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

editorials.title: An $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon
editorials.passage:
F ollow the money. If you want to know how the tech giant Meta really feels about the $18bn it agreed to fork out to end a landmark lawsuit against it – an outcome widely hailed as a victory for campaigners – just look at its share price . It didn’t go down when word came on Wednesday that Meta had settled with the 29 US states that had argued that the company’s Facebook and Instagram platforms harmed children. On the contrary, Meta stock went up, initially surging by 5%, before levelling out at a gain of just over 1.25%. There could be no clearer proof that the money men reckon Meta dodged a bullet.

To be sure, there was plenty to hearten those who have long believed that social media damages teenagers especially, whether by exposing them to content they shouldn’t see or by sapping their self-esteem, offering them filters that show how much prettier they would look if they had cosmetic surgery or giving them a metric of their popularity – and unpopularity – in the form of a running tally of “likes” and views.

For one thing, $18bn is a lot of money. For another, Meta has agreed to a series of changes in the way young people use their platforms . There’ll be a two-hour daily cap on use; restricted access during the night and the school day; likes will not be shown automatically and assorted safety and parental supervision measures will no longer be opt-in extras but the default standard. You can see why Lori Schott of Colorado, who believes the content her daughter encountered on Instagram played a part in her suicide aged 18, declared Wednesday to be “a good day” .

But look closer and you see that, for Meta, $18bn is not exactly a bank-breaking sum. It amounts to less than a month’s revenue . And it has 10 years to pay it out: the monthly payments could come out of petty cash. What’s more, nearly a third of that sum is contingent on Meta’s rivals YouTube and TikTok agreeing to the same restrictions. All told, the financial penalty is less than a tenth of the $200bn the 29 states were seeking, and a tiny fraction of the $1.4tn the company told the court it feared it would have to cough up . No wonder Meta’s shareholders were doing fist bumps on Wednesday.

Beyond the money, Meta will be thankful it has escaped a court ruling against it, a legal verdict on the behaviour detailed so compellingly in the California courtroom in the first week of the trial before it was abruptly halted. Jurors heard from the former Meta safety engineer Arturo Béjar, who spoke of his own teenage daughter’s experience on Instagram – how she received unwanted sexual advances, crude misogynistic insults and photos of male genitalia on the platform – and of a survey he had conducted that found 51% of teen users had had bad or harmful experiences on Instagram within the previous seven days, and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time. Béjar reported his findings to Mark Zuckerberg directly, but got no reply. As Béjar told me when we spoke on Thursday: “They knew that harm to kids was happening, but they were telling the world it wasn’t.” Under Wednesday’s settlement, Meta hasn’t even made an admission of liability.

As for the new restrictions, anyone who has seen a teenager on a computer or phone will have little confidence that they won’t find a way around them. If they do, then, according to this week’s deal, Meta will not be accountable. And crucially, says Béjar, it is Meta itself that still gets to define what constitutes harm.

No less frustrating, these new terms apply inside the US only, even though Meta’s reach, and its capacity to do damage, is global. As the gagged former Facebook employee Sarah Wynn-Williams described in her riveting book Careless People , the company was assiduous in hunting for new users in those overseas territories with few legal safeguards. There’s a parallel here with the tobacco industry: long after the US and Europe had cracked down on cigarettes, big tobacco was energetically selling into developing countries that had not yet put up their defences.

Above all, this week’s settlement addresses only the safety of children, despite the copious evidence of danger to adults, whether in the form of addiction or exposure to toxic misinformation. The danger lies not in this or that specific feature, but rather in the fundamental business model of social media: namely, tracking and surveilling individuals online, using the data gathered to construct a profile, which is then sold to advertisers eager to target potential consumers with extraordinary precision.

It’s this model that keeps users hooked, scrolling for hour after hour, as they are served content aimed directly at their interests and anxieties. As Ravi Naik, the lawyer who acts for Wynn-Williams and others, told me: “The algorithm preys on you.” The trouble with this latest settlement, he explains, is that “it reaches the features of Meta’s platforms but not the engine that drives them. The recommendation algorithm is untouched.”

What, then, can be done? For Béjar, the answer is to approach social media as a public health crisis, akin to the road traffic accidents that led to mandatory safety belts in cars (and not only for children). Governments need to say that any company involved in this crisis has to be involved in tackling it. And no one should fall for the line that the nature of the internet is such that it cannot be subject to meaningful regulation. When the music industry objected to copyright infringements online, incentives were swiftly arranged to fix the problem. As Béjar so damningly puts it: “A song has more protection than a kid.”

There are ample other precedents that can serve as guides to action, though none of them will please the titans of big tech. For decades, they have avoided being viewed as publishers, liable for what appears on their platforms. Nor do they want to be treated like carmakers, responsible for product safety. And they don’t like being likened to cigarette firms, selling a product they know is dangerous. Perhaps policymakers need to make a new comparison.

More than a century ago, when Standard Oil’s de facto monopoly was deemed harmful to consumers, it was broken up by order of the US supreme court into 34 smaller companies. Meta operates like a monopoly, with users feeling they can’t move, because all their friends and contacts are on the same few platforms. “Meta knowingly exploit this and refuse to make changes to their platforms that they know would deliver safer user experiences,” Damian Collins, a former chair of the UK parliamentary committee that oversees the digital realm, told me. If users could move their data and contacts over to new services, giving them more options, “break-up would work”.

This week’s settlement has been a disappointment to those longing to see the tech giants finally brought to heel, found guilty by courts and made to pay for it with costs too big to ignore. For now, Meta has swerved judgment day. But that day must surely come.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis
editorials.passage:
A s a Nepali citizen working on international climate policy for more than a decade, it is difficult to look at the harrowing images coming out of the catastrophic flash flood that thundered down valleys in Nepal, sweeping down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, and not feel angry.

Not just because of the destruction, but because it comes after years of warnings from scientists and civil society that a rapidly warming planet would make disasters more frequent, more intense and harder to predict. This is what the cost of delaying global climate action looks like.

On 26 August , a wall of ice, water, rock and mud tore through communities, destroying homes, markets, bridges, roads and hydropower infrastructure in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of people were killed and many more remain missing. The devastation came with terrifying speed. For people living along the rivers and the tourists trekking in the hills, there was little time between the hazard emerging high in the mountains and destruction reaching the valleys below.

The immediate questions are rightly being asked about what happened and whether people could have been warned. Nepal needs stronger early warning systems, better monitoring of glaciers and unstable slopes, cross-border communication between Nepal and Tibet and greater investment in preparedness.

But Nepal’s flash floods expose something more fundamental: the problem is not the absence of a warning system – it is a climate crisis that is producing hazards that behave differently from those the systems were designed to detect.

The warning system in the high-mountain Bhotekoshi valley illustrates the problem. The sudden, debris-laden flood destroyed upstream hydrological stations before they could register a rising water level and trigger an alert . The system was designed to detect a more gradual rise in water levels. This flood arrived as a massive surge of rock, mud and water, destroying the very instruments meant to detect it.

Preliminary assessments indicate that a large glacial collapse triggered an ice-rock avalanche and debris flow , temporarily blocking the river before a massive surge travelled downstream. The precise sequence is still being investigated. Whatever the final scientific explanation, the event shows how quickly hazards can cascade in a warming mountain environment.

By the time authorities received information about the flood and warnings were sent downstream, communities closest to the source had virtually no time to respond . The monitoring infrastructure did not simply fail to communicate the warning. It was destroyed before it could see the flood coming. That distinction matters. An early warning system designed around yesterday’s floods can be dangerously inadequate for tomorrow’s extremes.

This does not make early warning futile. It means we need to be honest about its limits. A warning is useful only if there is time to act. It cannot stop a mountain of ice and rock from collapsing. It cannot protect infrastructure in an increasingly hazardous corridor. And it cannot bring back a home, a hydropower station or a livelihood once it has disappeared.

Adaptation has limits, too . For years, Nepal and other vulnerable countries have been ramping up efforts to adapt: by strengthening infrastructure, improving preparedness, and protecting livelihoods – but often without financial support from the countries that historically contributed most to the climate crisis through historical emissions.

Nepal needs much greater international support for adaptation: early warning, mountain monitoring, climate science, anticipatory action, resilient infrastructure and disaster preparedness. Because Himalayan hazards originate beyond national borders, this must also include stronger cross-border cooperation and timely sharing of information.

The Nepal Himalaya is changing rapidly . Glaciers are retreating, while warming is altering the conditions in which glaciers, permafrost and mountain slopes remain stable. The climate in which these hazards occur is changing, and continued warming will make an already difficult risk landscape harder to manage. That is why the global response cannot stop at adaptation.

The first task must be to stop making the crisis worse. The countries that benefited most from decades of fossil fuel-driven growth have a particular responsibility to cut emissions rapidly. They also have far greater resources to do so. A just transition away from coal, oil and gas towards renewable energy is therefore a matter of global justice.

The fossil-fuel industry cannot be separated from this conversation. Companies have made enormous profits extracting and selling the fuels that have driven global heating, while communities on the climate frontline are being asked to prepare for increasingly destructive impacts with far fewer resources. Even rapid mitigation cannot undo the warming already baked into the climate system or immediately reverse changes already taking place in the Himalaya.

There is also a lesson for Nepal. It should not copy the economic model that created the climate crisis and call it development. We have an opportunity to build something different: an economy that puts people, livelihoods and ecological resilience before extraction.

The second task requires historical polluter states to pay for loss and damages. Nepal has contributed less than 0.1% of historical global greenhouse gas emissions. Its per-capita emissions remain among the lowest in the world. Yet we are increasingly paying for a crisis we did almost nothing to create. There is something profoundly unfair about this.

The cost of such an event is not an abstract figure in a post-disaster risk assessment. It is the lives of people killed by the flood; a hydropower station that took years to build and disappeared in minutes; livelihoods; public money that must now be spent on recovery instead of health and education.

Nepal and other vulnerable countries have repeatedly called on developed countries for compensation. The country should not be forced to borrow to recover from disasters to which it contributed so little. Nor should its scarce domestic resources repeatedly be diverted to repair damage caused by emissions of the global north.

Loss and damage finance must therefore be additional to existing official development assistance, adaptation and mitigation finance. It needs to be accessible and predominantly grant-based. But it cannot substitute for mitigation. No amount of compensation will be enough if the world continues to burn fossil fuels at the scale it does today. No adaptation programme can keep pace indefinitely with a climate that becomes more dangerous every year.

The people living along the Bhotekoshi river did not choose a warming Himalaya. They did not choose the fossil-fuel economy that drove most of the warming. However, with enough support, they can prepare better and build more resilient livelihoods. Sadly, they cannot adapt their way out of every disaster. This is why loss and damage finance is not charity – it is an obligation to people already paying the price.

Sunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, Nepal

editorials.title: Dolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying president
editorials.passage:
I’m still grieving Dolly Parton . I never met her and always wanted to. She was almost exactly my age and my height and had values I deeply admired. Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.

Which brings me to the person whose values are as far from Dolly Parton’s as any human could possibly be and still claim to be human. I’m referring, of course, to the current occupant of the Oval Office.

“I knew her a little bit,” Trump boasted about Parton on Glenn Beck’s radio show. “She really liked me, I will tell you!” at which Beck laughed out loud.

Trump has become mad as a hatter. Loonier than looney tunes. Totally nuts. An enraged, engorged child who’s frightened to death of being seen as a loser.

He’s losing his war in Iran – the war he decided to start without consulting Congress , without even telling the American people his goal or exit strategy.

Now he’s trapped there – with a stronger and more extreme group in control of Iran than before his attack, probably more intent on making a nuclear bomb, blocking the strait of Hormuz (it was open before Trump attacked), causing oil prices to rise again.

His current attempt to stop other countries from dealing with Iran is a bad joke. Iran is becoming the dominant power in the Gulf, having demonstrated its ability to damage the oil and gas infrastructure of its neighbors.

Besides, China can supply almost everything Iran needs and has a strong incentive to do so.

So – now clearly revealed as a loser – what does Trump do? Like any bully, he lashes out.

If the courts won’t allow him to put his name on the Kennedy Center, he’ll demolish it . If they say he doesn’t have authority to build his ballroom, he’ll fight to build it anyway .

If his blue paint on the reflecting pool is peeling and the green algae are back and his US attorney won’t prosecute “vandals” for causing the problem, he’ll stick to his story and blame vandals anyway .

It’s all going so badly for Trump that his lizard brain is compelled to show he can bully someone . So who does Trump choose? Our old neighbor and friend Canada , who has always gone along with whatever the American colossus ever wanted.

Trump imposed 50% tariffs on all cars, trucks, auto parts and steel coming from Canada.

Why? Because, he says : “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years. On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”

In other words, we’re in a trade war with Canada because, well, Trump wants one. A trade war with Canada probably seemed easier to win than a hot war with Iran. And he had to save face somehow , right?

Even though the supreme court found his attempt to use emergency powers for his last round of tariffs to be unconstitutional , he’s now using the Hawley-Smoot Tariff Act of 1930 – which, not incidentally, worsened the Great Depression.

But maybe a trade war with Canada won’t be all that easy to win. Canada has now retaliated with its own tariffs of up to 50% against about 700 American products .

As the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, noted on Saturday : “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so they can own us, and I promised that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”

Carney is now a hero in Canada with approval ratings in the 60s, while Trump’s have sunk to the low 30s .

Humiliation upon humiliation for the man who can’t stand to be humiliated.

It gets worse by the day.

Netanyahu has rejected Trump’s plan for Gaza. Congressional Republicans are blasting him for increasing imports of ground beef.

Universities are rejecting his latest directives. ABC has sued his regime for threatening its broadcast licenses.

Even the bond market won’t be cowed. It’s in open revolt against his bonkers fiscal policies.

Thank goodness for him that Darline Graham won South Carolina’s special election Republican runoff to replace her brother. Trump had made her race all about himself – of course – telling supporters that her opponents were “only fighting Darline because they want me to lose”.

I’m sure that’s what he’s telling himself about his many losses and humiliations – that they’re all due to his opponents plotting and scheming against him.

(Hopefully, he’s about to lose Congress, too.)

That’s an easier story for Trump to accept than the truth: that his carefully cultivated aura of invincibility has just about disappeared.

The would-be emperor has no clothes. Almost everybody now sees the thin-skinned, peevish, petty, incompetent, corrupt, naked infant who’s been parading around in presidential garb.

And they’re not going to obey him any more.

Dolly Parton was a huge winner, bless her soul. Trump is the biggest loser on the planet.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

editorials.title: The Home Office must not be allowed to bury the spycops inquiry
editorials.passage:
I n June 2013 Peter Francis, a former Metropolitan police officer, broke a 20-year silence about the role he had played in surveilling the family of Stephen Lawrence in a documentary jointly made by the Guardian and Channel 4’s Dispatches programme . Two years later, thanks in part to the programme, the Home Office established an undercover policing inquiry , commonly known as the spycops public inquiry, to shed light on the scale of surveillance of activists and trade unionists. That inquiry is now under threat.

Francis had served in the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Met unit founded in 1968 whose officers lived for years at a time inside political and campaigning organisations under false names.

In the months after Stephen Lawrence ’s murder in 1993 Francis had been deployed to pose as an anti-racist campaigner. His superiors pressed him to find “dirt” that could be used against the Lawrence family and their supporters. Stephen’s mother, Doreen, told the Guardian and Channel 4 that nothing she had heard since her son died had topped the revelation that police had been spying on her while she grieved. She had always suspected the police were watching. She never had proof.

The Lawrences were not an isolated case. Justice campaigns and trade unionists across the country were also monitored.

At least 139 officers adopted fake names, pretending to be political activists, to spy on people between 1968 and at least 2010. Dozens of anti-racist campaigners, family members of victims of police violence and leftwing activists have been surveilled by police.

Suresh Grover, whose Monitoring Group stood behind many of these victims of police surveillance, has told the inquiry that the suspicion directed at Black campaigners was rooted in racist stereotyping. Complaints from Black communities were treated as a public order threat in a way that identical complaints from others were not.

The government has justified the consultation they launched on 16 July into the future of the inquiry on the grounds that it has gone on for more than 11 years and cost £137m. The figures are accurate but their explanation is missing.

Applications for anonymity and restriction orders, the vast majority sought by police officers, have slowed down this inquiry. Litigation over cover names, and a persistent unwillingness among former officers and their commanders to say what they did has also hampered the process. The Met, which ran the SDS, made the inquiry slow and expensive. The same government department that funded and served the squad now cites the inquiry’s slowness and expense as reasons to cut it short.

Despite a push to wind up the inquiry, it is still producing revelations about the conduct of England’s police forces. Just last year, it revealed that an undercover officer, James Thomson, who had deceived two women into intimate relationships, was suspected of fabricating an elaborate plot to link an anti-foxhunting activist to a gun that he told managers the activist intended to collect in France.

Before the inquiry, Thomson’s managers admitted that in order to protect the SDS, nothing was done either about his intimate relationship with women he was surveilling or his possible fabrication of evidence. The unit, it seemed, trumped almost anything.

The inquiry also exposed numerous instances in which managers appeared to have knowledge of undercover officers having had sexual relationships that continued long after undercover deployments ended, in one case even after the announcement of the inquiry .

Another shocking discovery from the inquiry is that the Met spent £2.5m hiding an officer – John Dines – from his former lover, going as far as to relocate him from New Zealand to Australia for that purpose.

For the spycops scandal to be possible courts had to be misled. Officers were arrested alongside activists, appeared in court under false names and in some cases gave evidence under them without the court being told.

Surveillance was not limited to political activists and victims of racist violence. The Met’s own investigation concluded that special branch and the security services fed material to construction companies that blacklisted more than 3,000 workers suspected of being members of trade unions.

More instances of misconduct may come to light in the future, which is all the more reason to keep the inquiry running. The consultation is scheduled to end on 20 September, but there is still time to write to the Home Office to make sure that the government knows your views.

An inquiry that was set up because the state spied on the parents of a murdered child should not be closed down because the state has heard enough about itself. Doreen Lawrence has been told for 33 years that the truth is coming if she will wait just a little longer. She – and other victims of spying – have waited long enough. The inquiry should finish the job it was given.

Imran Khan KC is a practising solicitor

editorials.title: Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her?
editorials.passage:
T he moment that the world found out that Dolly Parton had died , I was in a hair salon in the reddest congressional district in New York state. The neighborhood on the shore of Lake Erie where I move every summer voted solidly for Donald Trump in 2024.

I often pass a lawn sign that has something misogynistic to say about New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, and the mere mention of Kamala Harris’s name can bring derisive jokes. Of course, there certainly are liberals and independents to be found, but on balance the area leans right.

On my errands around town, I’ve heard scornful comments about transgender people, and the local Catholic church where I sometimes attend mass has a priest who, during a homily this summer, praised Trump for his war in Iran.

A lot of the people I’ve chatted with around town are outspoken about being anti-vaccine.

But when cellphones started pinging with the news about Dolly, it’s not overstating things to say that everybody was devastated. Stylists and customers alike seemed to feel a personal connection – to her music, to her philanthropy, to her sheer goodness.

How did Dolly, a rags-to-riches country music superstar with a Tennessee twang and bedazzled everything, manage to endear herself to Americans of every political stripe?

What was her secret – and does it hold some wisdom for the those who seek unity in this divided nation, who appreciate civility, who believe there’s an American ethos that transcends our ugly politics?

Some of it, surely, was that she had a gift for poking fun at herself, and joining in the laughter, as when she would say she didn’t mind being called a dumb blonde because she knew, after all, that she wasn’t dumb – and that she wasn’t a blonde. After her illness made headlines last year, she took to social media to make a simple point: “I ain’t dead yet.” She called herself a “Backwoods Barbie” in a song of that name.

Then there was her remarkable generosity. Her organization, Imagination Library, gave more than 330m books to children around the world. She founded it, in part, she said, because her father couldn’t read or write.

She never forgot where she came from, as she raised money for a new hospital in her home country in Tennessee, or offered $500 awards to local teenagers when they graduated from high school.

Still, how did she manage not to alienate the Maga world when she promoted the Covid-19 vaccine (the research for which she had helped fund)?

Again, the humor helped, as when she changed the words of one of her most famous songs, Jolene to something that rhymed, and sang “vaccine, vaccine” in promotional videos. You had to smile, and maybe decide to get the jab, or at least to tolerate those who did. And she never made it political.

“She practiced a unique brand of radical acceptance,” wrote Jad Abumrad in a New York Times essay this week. “No one would ever be thrown out of the Big Dolly Tent.”

And, though she is being mourned as something of an angel on earth, she was a razor-sharp businessperson. She was smart and savvy about it all, as befitted the superstar who chalked up 25 No 1 country singles over the years.

As Abumrad learned while interviewing and observing her at length as he created the podcast Dolly Parton’s America, she always told her own story.

“If a male talkshow host made a joke about her figure, she’d make an ever better joke about it. She was always two steps ahead of you. She never allowed herself to be a part of a story of which she was not the author.”

Can what Dolly Parton did be bottled somehow? Can her serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity be sprinkled over our troubled waters to calm and soothe them?

Probably not – there is only one Dolly Parton – but that doesn’t mean we can’t learn something from this rare individual.

The rest of us might channel Dolly a bit more, and remember that a self-deprecating joke goes a long way toward easing tensions. We might recognize that financial success need not turn into ego glorification or arrogance.

And most of all, we might keep in mind that genuine generosity – if it comes from the heart – has the power to transcend politics.

Dolly Parton’s legacy, of course, resides in her wonderful songs, from Coat of Many Colors to 9 to 5. That’s what she would want.

But I don’t think she’d object if we also kept in mind her authentic kindness, her disarming wit – and the “radical acceptance” that fueled it all.

Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

editorials.title: Sri Lanka has one last chance to become a strategic hub in Indian Ocean
editorials.passage:
T he sight of over a dozen Iranian oil tankers gathered off the Sri Lanka n coast , together with the sinking of an Iranian vessel by a United States submarine in March , has once again placed the nation at the centre of a geopolitical crisis far beyond its shores. More importantly, it has highlighted something Sri Lanka has too often taken for granted: its geography. The island sits astride some of the world’s busiest sea lanes. Throughout history, its location has given Sri Lanka a strategic importance disproportionate to its size. The Portuguese, Dutch, and British understood this. During the Second World War, Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten established his South East Asia Command headquarters in erstwhile Ceylon. The island also played a crucial role in maintaining Allied communications and supply lines across the Indian Ocean. One of the most remarkable reminders of that role was the famous “Double Sunrise” service. From 1943, Qantas Catalina flying boats operated between Australia and Sri Lanka , maintaining an air link after the fall of Singapore. The flights were so long that crews and passengers saw two sunrises. As the 8 3rd anniversary of the service is commemorated, it is worth recalling that Sri Lanka once served as an indispensable logistical link across the Indian Ocean.

The question is whether the country can do so again. What Sri Lanka lacks Sri Lanka today possesses three extraordinary maritime assets. Colombo has become one of the world’s important transhipment centres, handling around 90 lakh TEUs a year, with a substantial share of its transhipment business connected to India. Trincomalee possesses one of the world’s great est natural harbours, with enormous potential for energy, storage, and industrial development. Hambantota is close to the main east-west maritime routes and offers land and deep-water capacity for industries that cannot easily be accommodated around Colombo. Together, these assets could form the foundation of something much larger: a logistics and energy hub in the Indian subcontinent comparable in concept, if not scale, to Rotterdam, Singapore, or Dubai. Yet , Sri Lanka has never fully realised this potential. Since independence, development has too often proceeded in fits and starts, driven by individual projects rather than a sustained national strategy. The country’s 30 -year war was another major impediment. It diverted resources, discouraged investment, and made long-term infrastructure planning and development far more difficult. I f Sri Lanka is to become a genuine multimodal hub, the airport too needs a major expansion, including a second runway. There is also an opportunity to rethink Colombo’s role as an aviation gateway to India. Under such an arrangement, Indian customs and immigration facilities could operate at Colombo airport, along the lines of arrangements at international airports elsewhere, making travel and onward connectivity more seamless. Such an arrangement would require detailed negotiations between the two governments, but the strategic objective must be clear: Colombo should function increasingly as an extension of the economic space in the Indian subcontinent and the Middle East . Sri Lankan Airlines must be privatised without further delay and placed with a strategic airline investor capable of developing Colombo as a n aviation hub for the Indian subcontinent and the Middle East. A national airline cannot be an end in itself; connectivity comes first . Trincomalee should become the centre of an integrated energy strategy. Its oil-storage capacity could be expanded and connected to India. Refining, petrochemical, and other energy-storage possibilities should also be examined. Combined with large-scale investment in the island’s wind and solar resources, such connectivity could transform Sri Lanka from an energy importer into an important regional producer of renewable electricity. editorials.title: Villages in UP, Gujarat & Kerala become towns differently. Why it matters for development

I ndia’s urban future is not being shaped only inside existing cities. Many rural settlements are turning urban in all but name. Agricultural land gives way to residential layouts and commercial activity; non-farm work expands; commuting and labour exchange extend beyond village boundaries; and expectations from local government increasingly resemble those of urban residents: piped water, drainage, solid waste management, better mobility. Urbanisation, therefore, often begins long before municipal notification. This reality is now finally reflecting in fiscal policy. The Sixteenth Finance Commission report, tabled this Budget, proposed a Rs 10,000-crore incentive—the Urbanisation Premium—for states to bring peri-urban villages into Urban Local Bodies. Each grant is to be calculated at Rs 2,000 per person in the area being incorporated, based on its Census 2011 population. More importantly, access to the premium is conditional on states preparing Rural to Urban Transition Policies. The Finance Commission expects these policies to identify transitional settlements and assess the implications of transition. This is significant because it shifts policy attention from what happens after a settlement becomes urban to what happens while it is becoming urban. This shift was long overdue.

The gap between the pace of settlement change and that of institutional change is a difficult governance problem. A settlement can acquire urban economic and spatial characteristics while continuing to be governed through a rural local body. The result is not simply a mismatch of labels. It can mean fragmented planning, weak land management, delayed infrastructure, limited fiscal capacity and growing pressure on institutions designed for a predominantly rural context. For residents, the consequences appear in concrete ways: unreliable water, poor drainage, congested roads, inadequate waste management and uneven access to urban services. The transition from village to town is consequently not just a question of jurisdiction, but of whether institutions can keep pace with changing human development needs. No one wants to fix this dirty secret 3 routes to urbanisation The 16th FC’s requirement that states have a Rural to Urban Transition Policy framework to unlock the Urbanisation Premium is valuable because it introduces the idea of anticipatory governance. Instead of waiting for notification and then trying to build municipal systems, states are being asked to identify transition areas and prepare in advance for their governance, financial and service-delivery needs. Yet the design of the Urbanisation Premium raises another question: is India’s transition to urban governance being imagined through too narrow an institutional pathway? The current recommendation is centred on merging villages with an adjoining ULB that already has a population of at least one lakh. That is an important pathway, but it is not the only way India becomes urban. The Constitution itself points to a more differentiated model. Article 243Q provides for a Nagar Panchayat for an area transitioning from rural to urban, a Municipal Council or Municipality for a smaller urban area and a Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area. It therefore does not assume that every settlement should make the same institutional jump. It recognises stages of urbanisation and provides different forms of urban local government. In 2011, nearly 73 per cent of Statutory Towns had populations below 50,000, falling in Census Classes III to VI. Therefore, a substantial part of India’s urban system consists of smaller settlements whose institutional capacity, fiscal base and service-delivery requirements are different. India’s actual transitions reinforce this diversity. Our analysis of more than 10,000 rural-to-urban institutional transitions recorded in the Local Government Directory (LGD) between 2013 and 2025 shows no single national pathway. At the national level, approximately 22 per cent of transitions moved into Municipal Corporations, 38.8 per cent into Municipalities and 37.2 per cent into Nagar Panchayats. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have predominantly expanded their urban landscape through Nagar Panchayats; Kerala has urbanised more through Municipalities; while Gujarat has seen a greater share of transitions associated with Municipal Corporations. These differences do not establish that one model is superior, but they do show that India’s urban transition is institutionally heterogeneous. And that matters for the design of Rural to Urban Transition Policies. A state where urbanisation is largely occurring through new Nagar Panchayats faces different questions from one where growth is being absorbed through existing municipalities or corporations. The relevant policy starting point is therefore not “how should a village become a municipality?” but “how is this state actually urbanising, and what institutional arrangement can govern that pathway?” Rural-to-urban transition should also be treated as a process rather than an event. Institutional change begins before notification and continues well after it. A serious transition policy should therefore identify emerging transition areas, assess readiness, prepare phased transition plans, strengthen staffing and financial systems, build technical capacity and protect continuity in services. Odisha’s Rural Urban Transition Policy 2023 offers a useful example. Rather than treating transition as a one-time act of municipal notification, it approaches it as a phased process of institutional preparation, bringing planning, governance, service delivery, administrative strengthening and stakeholder engagement into the transition itself. The wider lesson is important: the challenge is not simply to change jurisdiction, but to build the capability to govern the settlement through that change.
