Economic Survey lists obstacles Getting rural-to-urban transition right The Urbanisation Premium gives states additional fiscal resources as well as an opportunity to rethink how rural-urban transition is governed. Six principles could guide Rural Urban Transition Policies. First, build policy on evidence, not assumptions. No two states urbanise in the same way. Before designing transition policies, states should understand how they transition. LGD records, state notifications, Census data and spatial growth patterns can reveal dominant institutional pathways and help states make choices suited to their own patterns of urbanisation. Second, define transition as a process, not an event. Policy should set out clear stages, from identifying emerging transition areas and assessing institutional readiness to preparing roadmaps, building technical and administrative capacity, strengthening financial systems, ensuring citizen participation and supporting institutions after notification. Third, strengthen India’s constitutional urban framework. States should invest across the entire continuum of ULBs. Newly constituted Nagar Panchayats may need intensive support to establish municipal systems, while expanding municipalities and corporations face different challenges of integration, planning and metropolitan governance. Fourth, shift the focus from institutional creation to institutional capability . Creating a ULB is only the beginning. Transition policies should prioritise staffing, financial and regulatory capacity, spatial planning and the delivery of essential urban services. Success should be judged by the institution’s ability to govern, not merely by its creation. Fifth, make rural-urban transition a state finance agenda. State Finance Commissions should become central partners in assessing the fiscal implications of different transition pathways and financing the capacity needed during transition. Fiscal planning and institutional transition must develop together if urbanisation is to remain sustainable. Finally, recognise that transition is ultimately about people, not places. The objective should not merely be to change administrative status, but to improve service delivery and people’s lives. Pallavi Laungani is a PhD student at O.P. Jindal Global University, researching rural-urban transitions in India. Tarun Arora is an Associate Dean and Associate Professor at O.P. Jindal Global University, specialising in economics, urban policy and public policy. Views are personal. (Edited by Asavari Singh)

The Constitution itself points to a more differentiated model. Article 243Q provides for a Nagar Panchayat for an area transitioning from rural to urban, a Municipal Council or Municipality for a smaller urban area and a Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area. It therefore does not assume that every settlement should make the same institutional jump. It recognises stages of urbanisation and provides different forms of urban local government. In 2011, nearly 73 per cent of Statutory Towns had populations below 50,000, falling in Census Classes III to VI. Therefore, a substantial part of India’s urban system consists of smaller settlements whose institutional capacity, fiscal base and service-delivery requirements are different.

India’s actual transitions reinforce this diversity. Our analysis of more than 10,000 rural-to-urban institutional transitions recorded in the Local Government Directory (LGD) between 2013 and 2025 shows no single national pathway. At the national level, approximately 22 per cent of transitions moved into Municipal Corporations, 38.8 per cent into Municipalities and 37.2 per cent into Nagar Panchayats. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have predominantly expanded their urban landscape through Nagar Panchayats; Kerala has urbanised more through Municipalities; while Gujarat has seen a greater share of transitions associated with Municipal Corporations. These differences do not establish that one model is superior, but they do show that India’s urban transition is institutionally heterogeneous. And that matters for the design of Rural to Urban Transition Policies. A state where urbanisation is largely occurring through new Nagar Panchayats faces different questions from one where growth is being absorbed through existing municipalities or corporations. The relevant policy starting point is therefore not “how should a village become a municipality?” but “how is this state actually urbanising, and what institutional arrangement can govern that pathway?” Rural-to-urban transition should also be treated as a process rather than an event. Institutional change begins before notification and continues well after it. A serious transition policy should therefore identify emerging transition areas, assess readiness, prepare phased transition plans, strengthen staffing and financial systems, build technical capacity and protect continuity in services. Odisha’s Rural Urban Transition Policy 2023 offers a useful example. The wider lesson is important: the challenge is not simply to change jurisdiction, but to build the capability to govern the settlement through that change. editorials.title: Bengal BJP’s Trinamoolification can prove costly in 2029
editorials.passage:

The biennial Vibrant Gujarat Global Summit was successfully marketed to project the contrast between a pro-business, swift-on-delivery state government under Modi’s chief ministership and the alleged corruption and policy paralysis of the central government under Manmohan Singh. Twelve years later, as Modi prepares for a historic fourth term in office, a resurgent Bengal model sold as effectively to the rest of India as the Gujarat model once was could do wonders for the party in 2029. But the ‘Trinamoolification’ of the BJP in West Bengal is not helping the party’s cause as the electorate that has enthusiastically voted the BJP to power in the state for the first time in history has already started asking: Has anything really changed on the ground?

The biennial Vibrant Gujarat Global Summit was successfully marketed to project the contrast between a pro-business, swift-on-delivery state government under Modi’s chief ministership and the alleged corruption and policy paralysis of the central government under Manmohan Singh.

Twelve years later, as Modi prepares for a historic fourth term in office, a resurgent Bengal model sold as effectively to the rest of India as the Gujarat model once was could do wonders for the party in 2029. But the ‘Trinamoolification’ of the BJP in West Bengal is not helping the party’s cause as the electorate that has enthusiastically voted the BJP to power in the state for the first time in history has already started asking: Has anything really changed on the ground?

Twelve years later, as Modi prepares for a historic fourth term in office, a resurgent Bengal model sold as effectively to the rest of India as the Gujarat model once was could do wonders for the party in 2029.

But the ‘Trinamoolification’ of the BJP in West Bengal is not helping the party’s cause as the electorate that has enthusiastically voted the BJP to power in the state for the first time in history has already started asking: Has anything really changed on the ground?

Historic mandate, early let-down? In 2011, Mamata Banerjee had stormed to power in West Bengal with her battle cry of ‘ poriborton (change)’, ending the 34-year rule of the Left Front government led by the CPI(M). Banerjee had promised to end the party-state model of the Left, as well as political violence and forced land acquisition for industrialisation, which the Left Front government had tried to do in Singur and Nandigram. Yet by the time she was unseated from power in May 2026, not only she had repeated some of the mistakes of the Left Front government but also added a few of her own. A big charge against her party workers was the widespread practice of taking ‘cut money’ or illegal commissions from government welfare schemes, ‘tolabaji’ or extortion from businessmen, transporters, and shopkeepers, and land-grabbing. For the BJP, which had never been in power in West Bengal, unseating the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress was a historic chance not just to undo the wrongs of the previous governments but to also make a mark as the first Hindu Right government. Instead, there are already murmurs of disappointment not just from the BJP’s detractors in the state but also from some of those who voted the party to power. A new report in The Telegraph , dated 6 August, said the “trio that felled the 15-year-old Trinamool Congress regime in Bengal” — namely extortion, highhandedness, and landgrab — are bouncing back despite the BJP’s “avowed zero-tolerance policy against corruption”. BJP sources told The Telegraph that dozens of complaints have already reached the party’s senior state leadership, “accusing a section of leaders, including a few MLAs in and around Calcutta and several districts, of replicating the syndicate culture of the former Trinamool government”. The report went on to say that Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has launched three toll-free helplines for complaints related to cut money, syndicate extortion, and illegal toll collection, and urged people to report such crimes. Three senior IPS officers have been transferred to the anti-corruption branch, and a source told the newspaper that the Bengal government would maintain round-the-clock surveillance on the activities of both its leaders and officials. The party, according to the report, has already expelled nearly 50 BJP leaders and removed more than 100 others over allegations of extortion and corruption, including working hand in glove with former Trinamool leaders. It is not just one newspaper report that has exposed the new Bengal government’s inability to put an end to the political culture of corruption and extortion. On 20 August, Scroll ’s political editor Shoaib Daniyal tweeted : “The Bengal BJP might have experienced one of the shortest honeymoon periods after an election win. The social media anger started within a few weeks and now even ABP Ananda is attacking BJP for ‘becoming worse than Trinamool in only a 100 days’”. Even the party’s supporters and insiders are alarmed at how fast perceptions have changed about the BJP in Bengal. Senior advocate of the Calcutta High Court and RSS swayamsevak Joydeep Sen told ThePrint that Bengal’s historic mandate was not just for the BJP but also against the Trinamool Congress. “BJP needs to be extra careful about even a miniscule replication of the TMC menace by its cadre base. Though some reports and social media posts on corruption under the new government are exaggerated, they are not wholly untrue. The government needs to address the corruption and extortion issues right away,” Sen said. What has made matters worse, as far as public perception goes, is the BJP going soft on the Trinamool Congress after the elections. A Frontline report said what has irked people is the “rapidity with which many top Trinamool leaders have been accommodated within the NDA for political convenience”. “At the State-level, the BJP government is perceived to be on good terms with the Trinamool legislators who, led by Ritabrata Banerjee, broke ranks with former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee and staked claim as the main opposition in the Assembly,” the report said. Also read: India has bent too far for Bangladesh. Tarique Rahman is testing us Promise of resurgent Bengal Being unable to manage the optics game in Bengal may not augur well for the BJP in the next general elections. Conversely, if BJP manages to contain corruption and fulfil its key election promise of bringing industr ies back to Bengal, it might help the party put up a Bengal model for all of India to see and admire. Economist and Economic Advisory Council member Sanjeev Sanyal has said that for a “Viksit Bharat”, a “Viksit Bengal” is necessary. “In order for you to have Viksit Bharat, you need to have a Viksit Eastern India and Viksit Bengal and Viksit Kolkata are key to this because effectively getting a major urban hub firing up in Eastern India and creating a network of high growth in urban centres,” Sanyal has said. Speaking during an interaction at Chittaranjan Bhavan in Delhi, West Bengal Finance Minister Swapan Dasgupta said that the state had spent nearly five decades in a “mood of permanent depression”, with a growing sense that it was no longer relevant to India’s economic growth story. Dasgupta said the challenge was not merely to attract capital but to change the mindset of Bengali entrepreneurs and enable local businesses to make the transition from small and medium-sized enterprises to the “big league”. If the new state government can meet that challenge, resurgent Bengal may well become the BJP’s big ticket for 2029. Deep Halder is an author and a contributing editor at ThePrint. He tweets @deepscribble. Views are personal. (Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)

editorials.title: Bangladesh is moving beyond Hasina. But where is its foreign policy headed?
editorials.passage:
F rench philosopher and writer Ernest Renan argued that forgetting is as necessary to a nation as remembering. The Argentine sociologist Elizabeth Jelin made a less serene proposition: public memory is contested work, shaped by “memory entrepreneurs” who decide which version of the past may govern the present. Bangladesh is now conducting a somewhat similar exercise through its post-Hasina foreign policy. The problem is not that it has kept the geopolitics of 1971 on the side to ‘move on’. It is that repudiating one custodian of 1971 – Sheikh Hasina – is beginning to give Bangladesh’s foreign policy borderline strategic machoism – the country is pushing itself to sleep with its killers – and it is asserted as the new normal. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first proposed visit to India offers the immediate peg. Preparations had begun, but the visit stalled after Hasina addressed a virtual press conference from New Delhi on 5 August, attacked Bangladesh’s government and promised to return. India said it had neither organised nor endorsed a private event, but Dhaka chose to see little distinction between endorsement and permission. It demanded Hasina’s extradition and insisted that a “propitious environment” must precede Rahman’s visit. So, how normal is the new normal? Forgetting is a political act Collective memory has been a serious scholarly pursuit since French philosopher Maurice Halbwachs described its social construction a century ago. Today, universities at Aberdeen, Tampere and SOAS teach the politics of memory through foreign policy, historical analogy, transitional justice and reconciliation.

Today, universities at Aberdeen, Tampere and SOAS teach the politics of memory through foreign policy, historical analogy, transitional justice and reconciliation.

Countries emerging from war have treated memory differently. After Franco’s death in 1975, Spain’s transition to democracy rested partly on the Pacto del Olvido – the pact of forgetting so that the country could avoid reopening the atrocities of the 1936-39 Civil War and stabilise democracy. It also deferred justice and left later generations to reopen graves, archives, and arguments if they deem fit. Spain showed that official silence could postpone memory, even if it didn’t abolish it altogether. France and Germany built reconciliation through acknowledgement, reparations, treaties, and institutions – not by pretending Verdun or occupation or Auschwitz had never happened. Of course, these are comparisons and not templates. Bangladesh has every right to practice reconciliation in a changed global landscape, but one is not sure how far this goes because Pakistan has never delivered the unambiguous apology Bangladesh has repeatedly sought. The 1974 tripartite agreement recorded Pakistan’s condemnation and “deep regret” for crimes that may have been committed; Pervez Musharraf expressed regret again in 2002. But regret is not acknowledgement. Bangladeshi lawyer and writer Khan Khalid Adnan aptly describes this as substituting regret for accountability. Even other countries like Turkey and Saudi Arabia, that Bangladesh courts today, have prioritised Pakistan’s stance in 1971, while China opposed the creation outright. Who owns 1971? The debate inside Bangladesh is richer than a binary contest between secularists and Islamists. Bangladeshi scholars identify two histories of liberation: one centred on the Awami League’s mandate and another on the longer popular, intellectual and military struggle. Both defend 1971, but what they dispute is its custodians. Bangladeshi journalist Mahfuz Anam makes the essential separation: Mujib’s role in liberation must be distinguished from his failures after 1972 and Hasina’s later authoritarianism. Hasina’s dynastic use of Mujib tied his image to coercion and reduced the Indian relationship to one built around the Awami League rather than Bangladesh. Breaking completely with Bengali nationalism could discard 1971’s emancipatory promise. Hasan Ferdous explicitly calls out India: New Delhi expects gratitude, while young Bangladeshis see Hasina as someone who violated the Liberation War’s democratic values. editorials.title: Punjab’s biggest IAS batch in 30 years has no real work. Govt is keeping them in waiting room
editorials.passage:
I ran into a colleague at a social function recently, and what came up as we got talking has stayed with me since. Ten IAS officers of the 2024 batch, by most reckoning the largest cohort assigned to Punjab in 30 years or more, have completed their Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) probation and district training. Not one of them has been posted as Sub-Divisional Magistrate. All 10 have instead been attached to their Deputy Commissioners as Officer on Special Duty, Urban Affairs. OSD is a designation more often used to park an officer awaiting posting than to assign one real work. These officers have been selected out of the several lakh who sit the Civil Services Examination each year for one of 180 seats. I’m told that the number of seats has remained the same since 2012. I am withholding my colleague’s name and posting history, at their request. What follows draws on what they told me, and on my own years as Deputy Commissioner, Financial Commissioner Revenue, Chief Administrator of PUDA, and Joint Secretary, Housing and Urban Affairs.

The office with a rudder The Sub-Divisional Magistrate holds magisterial powers under the criminal law, collector’s powers under the land law, and supervisory charge of the Tehsil and Development Block beneath. The SDM is also Returning Officer at Assembly elections, Land Acquisition Collector when the State needs land, registering authority for a hundred kinds of deeds, and the first point of contact when a citizen’s grievance runs from a disputed boundary to an unregistered death. Three things an SDM has that an OSD does not: a jurisdiction, a statute, and a queue outside the door. Put differently — and here I will allow myself the one metaphor this piece needs — the SDM’s post is a ship, however modest the tonnage: a hull, a rudder, a crew, a course to steer, and open water on which to run aground and learn from it. An OSD posting, however dignified the file cover, is a wheel bolted to a wall. Turn it as often as you like. Nothing moves. My colleague’s own first months illustrate exactly what is being denied to this year’s 10. As an Assistant Commissioner Under Training (ACUT, that peculiar acronym under which every one of us has done our early penance), their Deputy Commissioner found a Block Development and Panchayat Officer’s post lying vacant and simply handed it over: here is an office, a jeep, a staff and an agenda; go and run it. No one asked whether the officer was ready. The post made them ready. Samrala, Dhar Kalan, and the two years My own first charge was Samrala, one of a handful of Punjab subdivisions that cadre convention, not statute, marked out as an “IAS subdivision” for direct recruits. Every such subdivision carries its own folklore. Samrala’s included IAS officer Rakesh Singh (1978 batch), later Chief Secretary, Punjab, and Amitabha Pande before him. Both are names any officer of my generation would recognise. Dhar Kalan carries a version of the same lore: carved out of the old Pathankot subdivision, for years the state’s smallest, and traditionally the freshest officer’s first charge: few villages, thin establishment, no glamour, but a magistrate’s court and citizens expecting a real answer. I don’t believe an officer of my experience could not name a similar subdivision of their own. What none of us had to contend with was a truncated tenure. We joined on 1 July, giving us full two years in the chair, long enough for the incoming batch to be trained and ready to step in by the time we left. Today’s recruits join on 1 January, which trims the same charge to about 18 months, even in years when it is given at all. The erosion started with the calendar, years before the batch of 2024 arrived. This year’s 10 are simply the first batch for whom it ran out entirely. Even the smallest, shortest SDM-ship is still a ship. An OSD’s desk, however large the district, has no vessel attached to it. OSD—officer, sans duty? I spent three years as Chief Administrator of Punjab Urban Planning and Development Authority (PUDA) and, later, as Joint Secretary in the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, helping draft what became the Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA). No one needs to convince me that urban governance matters, or that it is increasingly the site of Punjab’s hardest administrative problems. If the government wants 10 fresh minds thinking about urban affairs, I am the last person to object. But that is not what an OSD (Urban Affairs) posting delivers, and everyone who has held or supervised one knows it. Where is the file that defines this officer’s agenda? Which municipal body reports to them, under what statute? What decision can they take that does not first require someone else’s signature? At best, each OSD will be just another staff officer attached to the Deputy Commissioner of the district, one more name on the list. They are being kept in a waiting room with an impressive nameplate on the door, and Punjab’s Municipal Committees and Corporations are no better administered for it. Also read: The case for Agnipath 2.0 — India needs a cheaper military, not a cheaper soldier Hand them the wheel Administrative reasons behind this year’s posting orders may not be apparent from outside the file. If so, the government owes these 10 officers, and the service, an explanation. What is at stake is the quality of administration in Punjab. A decade from now, when these officers will become Deputy Commissioners and Financial Commissioners themselves, they wouldn’t have the learned ropes one does in the early years of the service. You cannot learn grievance redressal without facing the public, crisis management from a briefing note, or what a revenue order costs a family by reading it after someone else has signed it. The state must give each of the 10 a jurisdiction. Give them a statute to administer and a public that knows where their office is. Give them the ship (however small the tonnage, however unglamorous the subdivision) rather than a wheel with nothing behind it. That is how this service has always made administrators. I see no reason, none yet offered, why the 2024 batch should be the first asked to learn it standing at the dock. The author is a retired IAS officer of the 1984 batch, Punjab cadre, who superannuated as Special Chief Secretary, Government of Punjab. Views are personal. (Edited by Ratan Priya)
