editorials.title: India’s first railway is disappearing bit by bit. Can we save what’s left?
editorials.passage:
The Great Indian Peninsula Railway – the GIPR – is the railway that operated India’s first commercial passenger line between Bombay and Thane in 1853. The Bombay-Thane line was not merely India’s first passenger railway route. It was the beginning of a system that transformed the country. The railway that began with three locomotives, 14 coaches and about 400 passengers on April 16, 1853. eventually grew into the vast Indian Railways network.

Today’s Central Railway suburban system in Mumbai still runs across much of that original landscape. That continuity is extraordinary. We should be proud of it. But pride cannot simply mean celebrating the first train every April 16 and then allowing the physical evidence of that story to disappear year after year.

This August, that question has arrived at Sion.

A portion of the old Sion railway station, on the original Bombay-Thane line of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway, is being dismantled to make way for railway expansion. Among the elements that could disappear along with the old station hut (used as station manager’s cabin) are old iron roof brackets bearing the imprint of the GIPR era.

I have appealed for at least some of these brackets to be carefully removed and preserved — at the heritage gallery at Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, the outdoor exhibition gully or the National Rail Museum in New Delhi. The Railway Board’s Heritage Directorate has acknowledged the appeal to save the Sion relics, while the Rail Enthusiasts’ Society has extended formidable support to the effort.

This is not the first time I have made such an appeal.

I have been fighting this battle for over three decades now.

Much of the original alignment of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway survives within today’s Mumbai suburban system. The trains have changed, the traction has changed, the stations have changed and the railway is now Central Railway. But the basic geography of that first line remains remarkably alive.

The relics here talk to tell the story of the first railway line which can be elaborately read in my first book Halt Station India, The Dramatic Tale of the Nation’s First Rail Lines .

Scattered along it are the last physical witnesses to that beginning.

Some are substantial structures. Others are tiny pieces of iron.

To most people, an old bracket may look like scrap metal. To me, a GIPR bracket carrying the company’s distinctive markings is a piece of the birth certificate of Indian Railways.

That is why the dismantling of the old Sion station structure now worries me deeply.

In 2017, when redevelopment was taking place at Bhandup, I similarly reported the demolition of the old Bhandup station hut along with its wrought-iron brackets bearing the GIPR logo. Bhandup was not just any suburban station. It was similarly one of the stations on the original Bombay-Thane line, and the first passenger train had made a watering halt there.

At Mumbra, demolition of the old hut in the east, along with brackets revealed another extraordinary survivor – a Victorian-era Tucker & Reeves wall safe embedded in the old booking office. There were efforts to save them, but not for long. All the relics may not have survived, but the discovery demonstrated precisely why demolition of old railway structures needs to be approached with an archaeological eye.

I wrote about both cases and pushed for the relics to be saved.

The result was encouraging. Central Railway decided to preserve the Bhandup GIPR brackets and the Mumbra safe, eventually moving them to the heritage gallery at CSMT. I don’t if they are still there, but those brackets and the safe were at the CSMT heritage museum for some days because somebody stopped the demolition process long enough to ask a simple question: What are we throwing away?

That question has followed me ever since my school days, when I discovered that the railways I had been travelling on (between Kurla and Matunga) was a part of India’s first line and the relics here were the central pieces of India’s railway heritage story.

I have repeatedly documented the surviving fragments of the GIPR – from old railway lamps and safes to GIPR plaques, electric-mast markings, signal structures, old tiles, stonework and roof brackets. Some were rescued. Some were documented. Some were lost.

I have learnt the hard way that heritage disappears piece by piece, project by project, work order by work order.

Kalyan provided another painful reminder. The station’s arched roof went in 2022. A year earlier in 2021, a roughly 168-year-old GIPR-era bridge near Shahad was dismantled and replaced because its steel structure had become dangerously corroded.

I understand completely that railway infrastructure has to remain safe. But when an original railway structure has to go, there should be a parallel obligation to document it properly and preserve representative components wherever possible.

Byculla, meanwhile, shows us what is possible when the approach is different. Byculla has an extraordinary place in railway history. The first railway passed through the area, and the station precinct is associated with the earliest years of the Bombay–Thane railway. During its restoration, original features were painstakingly identified and restored in the west side. That is the lesson.

Modernisation and heritage conservation do not have to be enemies. The railway can add tracks and still save a bracket. It can demolish an unsafe structure and still retain a representative section. It can replace a bridge and still preserve a girder, plate, maker’s mark or other historically significant component. What is required is awareness before the excavator arrives.

Sion is particularly important

Sion is not an arbitrary railway location. The first sod (the foundation stone) for the GIPR line was ceremoniously turned near Sion on October 31, 1850. The Indian Railways itself records this association, noting that the first sod for the GIP line from Bombay to Kalyan was turned at a place near Sion.

The first railway line subsequently ran through this landscape, linking Bombay with Thane and eventually becoming the foundation of not just the enormous Central Railway suburban system that exists today, but Indian Railways as a whole.

So when the old Sion railway structure carrying GIPR imprints disappears in August, it is not simply an old building being demolished, but a fragment of the physical landscape associated with the birth of Indian Railways is disappearing.

And this time there is an important difference. The Railway Board’s Heritage Directorate has acknowledged the appeal to save the Sion brackets. That acknowledgment matters.

It means the issue has reached precisely the part of the railway establishment that exists to recognise and protect such history.

The Rail Enthusiasts’ Society has also extended formidable support to the effort. It has also acknowledged that these are not merely objects of nostalgia but tangible pieces of India’s industrial history. There is therefore an opportunity to turn an appeal into action.

We cannot save everything. But we can save something. I have never argued that every old railway object must remain exactly where it stands.

That would be unrealistic. Mumbai’s suburban railway is a living, heavily congested system. It carries millions of passengers and has to expand. Tracks have to be added, bridges rebuilt, stations remodelled and obsolete structures removed. I understand that better than most. Safety is paramount.

But I also believe that development cannot be allowed to erase memory.

The answer is documentation and selective preservation. Put it somewhere where the next generation can see it, the central pieces of India’s industrial heritage.

The Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus heritage gallery itself is proof that this can work. I had been involved in originally setting it up years ago, listing and taking old relics there. These objects tell a story that no textbook can tell quite as powerfully.

A child looking at a GIPR relic in a museum can understand that this was once physically attached to a railway building through which the earliest trains of India passed. That is living history. Mumbai is ground zero of Indian railway history. That is the reason I keep returning to this subject.

We need a systematic GIPR heritage programme for Mumbai, start with a basic plaque at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, acknowledging its role. I have been arguing for this for years.

A proper documentation and inventory should identify the surviving structures and movable relics along the original GIPR alignment – from Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (formerly Victoria Terminus) and Byculla through Sion, Bhandup and Thane and onwards to the later extensions towards Kalyan and beyond.

Every surviving relic should be photographed, mapped, catalogued and graded. Those of exceptional significance should be protected in situ wherever possible. Those that cannot remain should be transferred to a museum or heritage gallery. And demolition proposals affecting known GIPR structures should automatically trigger a heritage review before work begins.

This is not about stopping the railway. It is about making the railway remember itself.

Sion gives us one more chance

I have seen too many of these pieces disappear. I have watched old railway fabric become debris. I have written about it, photographed it, argued about it, appealed to railway officials and, sometimes, succeeded in getting something saved. Sometimes I have failed.

I am therefore making this appeal once again. For the generations that will one day ask, “Where did India’s railway begin and what remains of it today”?

Rajendra B Aklekar is the author of several books on India's rail history and transport heritage. They include Halt Station India, India’s Railway Man: A Biography of E. Sreedharan A Short History of Indian Railways. This article first appeared on his website.

editorials.title: China just jailed a corrupt billionaire for life. Could that ever be possible in India?
editorials.passage:
Welcome to The India Fix by Shoaib Daniyal. A newsletter on Indian politics.

As always, if you’ve been sent this newsletter and like it, to get it in your inbox every week, sign up here (click on “ follow ”).

Hui Ka Yan was once China’s richest person. On August 20, the Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court sentenced him to life in prison for bribery, swindling public funds and fraud, among other charges. The order also confiscated all of Yan’s personal property, levied fines of more than $2 billion on corporations once controlled by him and sentenced five other senior executives, including Hui’s two sons, to prison terms ranging from six to 18 years.

A week later, a tribunal in India passed an order on another disgraced billionaire. Unlike China, though, India was much softer. Zee TV founder Subhash Chandra owed his creditors, including state-owned firms, Rs 22,007 crore ($2.3 billion). But the National Company Law Tribunal approved a plan that allows Chandra to pay back only a little more than Rs 6 crore – 0.03% of what he owed.

Angry creditors say there are infirmities in the process, alleging links between people voting for this plan and Chandra. They also claim that Chandra has managed to significantly underreport his assets. But now that the tribunal has given its stamp of approval on this absurdly small recovery amount, there might be little they can do. The money, including those from taxpayer-funded, state-owned firms, that Chandra has borrowed might be lost for good.

China and India are neighbours with much in common, including almost identical population sizes. Yet, their dissimilar approaches towards billionaires might partly explain why their economic fortunes have diverged so much over the past decade.

China regularly targets and even jails billionaires. So much so that Ruchir Sharma in the Financial Times writes that it might be “dangerous” to be too rich in a country whose government’s stated goal currently is “common prosperity”.

As the contrast between Hui and Chandra shows, there is no such fear south of the Himalayas. In India, billionaires accused of fraud rarely face criminal action. In fact, there have been prominent examples of billionaires being allowed to comfortably escape India and, hence, legal action. On Thursday, Vijay Mallya, now living in London, even congratulated his “friend Subhash”, pointing out that he had, in fact, done a better job of paying back his debts than the media tycoon.

Indian social media has been outraging over the absurd unfairness of what happened. The leniency shown to Chandra would be unthinkable when it came to a regular Indian citizen. Thousands of Indian farmers die by suicide every year, a major reason for which is inability to pay off their debts . Worse, a large chunk of this money lent to billionaires has been siphoned off from public sector banks, meaning the government has to eventually foot the bill – an egregious crime in a poor country like India which struggles to garner funds for development and welfare.

Moreover, this leniency shown to billionaires in India is more than just a moral failure: it points to a feature of the political economy that has harmful economy-wide effects. Billionaires have so much power over the Indian state it might be end up stifling economic growth itself.

Indians can plainly see oligopolies develop in major sectors. Data shows that aviation, telecom, cement, steel, and tyres saw market concentration hit unprecedented levels. It’s so bad that even the Indian government has flagged the “oligopolistic nature” of the country’s aviation sector.

Economists Arvind Subramanian and Josh Felman cheekily call this India’s “2A model”, referencing what appear to be the Modi government’s two favourite billionaires: Gautam Adani and Mukesh Ambani. The “generous and extensive favours granted to big business houses (especially Adani and Ambani)”, they write, “allowed them to prosper at the expense of other investors, domestic and foreign”.

In theory, a free market should see firms add value and create wealth. But, as a book co-authored by Subramanian points out, if all it takes to succeed in the market is “regulatory favours” as a result of being “seen close to the government”, it can actually be at the “cost of wealth creation by other less-connected firms”.

The result, Subramanian and Felman argue, has been a “non-level playing field” that has “extracted a toll, discouraging overall investment in the industrial sector”.

It’s so bad that former Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Viral Acharya has even proposed breaking up India’s five biggest industrial firms to end the investment freeze and lower inflation. He calls the current dominance an example of “crony capitalism” arising out of “political connections”.

Recently, commerce minister Piyush Goyal highlighted this difference between how India and China treat billionaires, in a pitch to Japanese investors. “You don’t have to worry that if you make money in India, if you are a successful businessman, you may disappear one day, and end up coming out as a professor in a Japanese university,” he said. “That risk doesn’t happen in India.”

Goyal was referring to Jack Ma, one of China’s richest people, who rarely appeared in public between October 2020 and January 2021 as the Chinese government conducted a regulatory crackdown on his businesses.

Unfortunately, such a simplistic understanding of the drivers of the economy is possibly why India’s net foreign direct investment has practically dropped to zero over the past few years.

editorials.title: Nepal floods are a warning: China’s mega-dams in Tibet should worry India
editorials.passage:
At approximately 8:40 am on Wednesday, August 26, catastrophic flash floods tore through the mountainous region along the Nepal-Tibet border, once again exposing the extraordinary vulnerability of the Himalayas to large-scale natural disasters. Current scientific assessments indicate that a large section of a Himalayan glacier collapsed, releasing enormous quantities of ice, rock, mud and debris. The collapse generated a powerful avalanche and debris flow that entered the river system, sending floodwaters surging downstream through the rivers.

The disaster has raised fears of an enormous human toll, with large numbers of people reported dead or missing and extensive damage to infrastructure. If the worst reports are confirmed, it could rank among the most devastating Himalayan disasters in recent history.

Beyond the immediate human tragedy, however, the catastrophe raises a much larger and increasingly urgent question: What happens when infrastructure of unprecedented scale is constructed in one of the most geologically fragile and environmentally unpredictable regions on Earth?

For years, China has been advancing plans for an enormous hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet. Often referred to as the Medog Dam or the Yarlung Tsangpo mega-dam, the project has attracted international attention because of its unprecedented scale, sensitive location and potential consequences for countries downstream.

The Yarlung Tsangpo originates on the Tibetan Plateau and flows eastward across Tibet before turning sharply south through one of the deepest river gorges in the world. It then enters India, where it becomes the Brahmaputra, before continuing into Bangladesh. The proposed hydropower development is located around Medog County, close to India’s Arunachal Pradesh.

Few places in the world offer comparable hydropower potential. Here, the river descends dramatically from the high Tibetan Plateau through narrow Himalayan valleys and deep gorges. The combination of enormous water volume and extraordinary vertical drop creates tremendous energy-generating potential.
That geographical advantage explains China’s ambitions. The project is expected to dwarf the Three Gorges Dam, whose installed generating capacity is approximately 22.5 gigawatts. Estimates surrounding the Yarlung Tsangpo project have suggested a generating capacity of around 60 gigawatts or more. If realised on that scale, it would become the largest hydropower development ever undertaken.

The investment involved is equally extraordinary, with estimates running to well over $100 billion, potentially making it one of the most expensive infrastructure projects in history. For Beijing, the project carries enormous strategic importance. China presents the development as part of its transition towards clean and renewable energy, reducing dependence on coal while expanding electricity supplies and supporting economic development. Hydropower generated in Tibet could also contribute to China’s broader strategy of transmitting electricity from the resource-rich western regions to major population and industrial centres in the east.
In that sense, Tibet is not only strategically important because of its territory, borders and natural resources. It could increasingly become an important energy production base for China. But the same geography that makes the Yarlung Tsangpo so attractive for hydropower also makes the region extraordinarily dangerous.

The Himalayas are among the youngest and most geologically active mountain systems on Earth. Earthquakes, landslides, glacial collapses, avalanches, extreme rainfall, glacial lake outburst floods and massive debris flows are recurring features of this landscape. Climate change is adding another layer of uncertainty as glaciers retreat and high-altitude environments undergo rapid transformation.
The August 26 disaster provides a stark illustration of how quickly events in these mountains can escalate. A collapse beginning high in the Himalayas can send millions of tonnes of ice, rock, mud and water into narrow river valleys. Once confined within steep gorges, these flows can accelerate dramatically, destroying almost everything in their path. Homes, bridges, roads, hydropower facilities, communications infrastructure and cross-border transport routes can disappear within minutes.

From the perspective of hydropower, the geography is extraordinary. From the perspective of disaster risk, the same geography presents an equally extraordinary challenge. The central question is therefore not simply whether China possesses the engineering capacity to construct such a project. It is whether any country can completely control the risks created when infrastructure of unprecedented scale is placed inside such a volatile natural environment.

The consequences also extend far beyond Tibet. The Yarlung Tsangpo-Brahmaputra is an international river system supporting communities across Tibet, India and Bangladesh. Millions of people depend directly or indirectly on its waters for agriculture, fisheries, ecosystems, transportation and economic activity. For India, the issue is particularly sensitive. The river enters India through Arunachal Pradesh, a region already at the centre of a longstanding territorial dispute between China and India. Beijing claims much of Arunachal Pradesh as part of what it calls “South Tibet”, while India administers the territory as an integral part of the country. The dam therefore sits at the intersection of three highly sensitive issues: water, energy and territorial security.

Indian officials have repeatedly expressed concern about the implications of enormous upstream infrastructure on the Brahmaputra. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu, among others, has publicly warned about the potential consequences for downstream communities. The concern is not simply that China is constructing a dam. It is that control over major upstream infrastructure inevitably gives the upstream state greater influence over the monitoring and management of river flows. In normal circumstances, such infrastructure may be managed for electricity generation and water regulation. But during an extreme natural disaster, technical failure, political confrontation or military crisis, the consequences could become far more serious. This is where the issue moves beyond environmental policy and enters the realm of national security.

Relations between China and India have remained deeply complicated since their 1962 war. Border disputes, competing regional interests, Tibet, military deployments and periodic confrontations along the Line of Actual Control continue to shape relations between Asia’s two largest powers. Against this background, India’s concern over the Yarlung Tsangpo project cannot simply be dismissed as opposition to Chinese economic development. For New Delhi, the question is ultimately one of vulnerability. If critical water infrastructure upstream is controlled entirely by another country, particularly a strategic competitor, downstream populations inevitably become concerned about what that control could mean during a future crisis.

The August 26 flash floods demonstrate a fundamental reality about the Himalayan region: nature does not respect political borders. A glacier can collapse in one territory, send a debris flow into another, destroy infrastructure downstream, disrupt international trade routes and threaten communities far beyond the place where the disaster began. The same principle applies to rivers. What happens upstream in Tibet does not necessarily remain in Tibet. Decisions involving the Yarlung Tsangpo can potentially affect communities across northeastern India and ultimately other countries. That is why the mega-dam cannot reasonably be viewed solely as a domestic Chinese energy project. It is also a transboundary environmental, humanitarian and geopolitical issue.

The latest Himalayan disaster should therefore serve as a warning. The question is not whether hydropower should exist in the Himalayas, nor whether China has the right to develop renewable energy. The more urgent question is whether a project of unprecedented scale can be developed safely and transparently in one of the world’s most geologically unstable regions without exposing downstream populations to unacceptable risks.

For India and Bangladesh, the answer cannot simply be to wait and see. They have strong reasons to deepen cooperation on river monitoring, satellite observation, early-warning systems, disaster preparedness, hydrological data sharing and diplomatic engagement with China. International institutions should likewise encourage greater transparency and meaningful consultation over projects whose consequences could cross national borders.

The Himalayas are sometimes described as the “Water Tower of Asia” because rivers originating on the Tibetan plateau sustain enormous populations downstream. Control of those waters therefore carries responsibilities that extend beyond any single country’s borders. China’s Yarlung Tsangpo mega-dam may ultimately become one of the greatest engineering achievements of the twenty-first century. But if environmental risks, geological instability, downstream interests and international cooperation are not adequately addressed, it could also become one of the region’s greatest sources of uncertainty.

We should all recognise that the flash floods are a warning of the potentially devastating consequences of China’s growing dam expansion across Tibet. Therefore, for the safety and security of tens of millions of people, the international community has a responsibility to speak out against and challenge China’s actions that could put downstream communities at risk.

(Lobsang Dakpa is a Tibetan writer, lawyer, and former Member of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile. He has previously served as the President of the Tibetan Legal Association and currently works as the Operations Director of the 108 Peace Institute. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: India-China consensus signals positive momentum, but don’t overstate its importance
editorials.passage:
Between the devastation in Nepal and the relentless clownery of Donald Trump, it is easy to lose sight of the winds of change in India-China ties, with Xi Jinping and Narendra Modi slated to meet twice in quick succession. Once on the sidelines of the August 31-September 1 Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where their paths may briefly cross. And more substantially in New Delhi for the BRICS Summit from September 12-13, when Xi is expected to arrive with a large delegation.

It is understandable that both sides are working hard on the possible deliverables for Xi’s first visit to India in seven years, and NSA Ajit Doval’s recent visit to Beijing — ostensibly to co-chair the India-China Special Representatives-level dialogue with Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi — should also be seen in this light.
That said, Doval’s visit underlined the subtle shift in the grammar of bilateral ties that is moving from controlled optics towards genuine engagement, with both sides settling on rare progress in boundary talks and an even rarer joint statement.
Yet we must not lose sight of the larger picture. The eight-point outcome document released on Wednesday following the meeting between Doval and Wang in Beijing reflects an ongoing recalibration in Asian geopolitics. After years of protracted military standoff and institutional estrangement along the LAC, New Delhi and Beijing are attempting to establish an operational equilibrium.

This diplomatic manoeuvre is occurring against the backdrop of sweeping changes in global geopolitics driven by the disruptive unilateralism of Donald Trump’s America. Confronted by the United States’ aggressive tariff regime, military adventurism, mercantile approach and structural instability in the multilateral trading order, both Asian powers face compelling structural incentives to stabilise their frontier.

As the Trump administration weaponises trade and recasts alliance networks, India and China face distinct vulnerabilities. China contends with accelerated technological decoupling and trade barriers, while India navigates punitive economic pressures, a prolonged energy squeeze, a secondary sanctions minefield as well as Washington’s stunning geopolitical pivot to Pakistan.
India and China seeking to inch closer, therefore, is one aspect of the cautious diplomatic thaw and economic reset undertaken by both sides to stabilise their bilateral relations. This effort acquires immediate urgency with the prospect of Xi’s visit to India next month (though Beijing is yet to officially confirm it), marking his first bilateral visit following the 2019 informal summit in Mamallapuram.

To ensure this high-stakes summit yields stability, both nations require a de-escalated border architecture and a reduction in persistent tension arising from differing perceptions of the LAC. However, an analysis of the diplomatic readouts surrounding the 25th round of SR-level talks between Doval and Wang reveals that the pathway to stability is paved with cautious incrementalism rather than comprehensive resolution.

Both sides released separate readouts of the Doval-Wang meeting on Tuesday, followed by a joint statement of outcomes the day after. The statements reveal distinct doctrinal positions.

The Chinese readout released on August 25 projects a procedural and phased approach. By stressing on a “package settlement” to the border issue, Beijing harks back to the 2005 agreement on ‘Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for the Settlement of the India-China Boundary Question’.

This framing implies a comprehensive territorial swap across all sectors simultaneously — an approach China has leveraged to compartmentalise the border dispute away from broader bilateral relations. This construct traditionally presumes an inter-sectoral trade-off across the western, middle and eastern sectors of the LAC.

New Delhi’s August 25 readout omitted any reference to ‘package settlement’. Instead, India’s statement asserted that both sides “agreed to continue their work in seeking a political settlement of the boundary question in the context of their overall and long-term interests”. This formulation reinforced India’s core strategic doctrine since 2020: the boundary dispute cannot be sequestered into a purely cartographic exercise.

The release of the joint eight-point outcome and consensus document on August 26 represented a rare instance of diplomatic convergence.

The eight-point consensus omitted the Chinese reference to a “package settlement”. India’s insistence on a “political settlement” of the boundary question was also set aside. The joint statement converged on “early and substantial harvest of boundary delimitation and border management”.

Last year, under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC), both sides had agreed to establish an expert group to explore an ‘early harvest’ in boundary delimitation in less contentious border areas. That formulation has now been formally upgraded to an “early and substantial” harvest, which may be interpreted as tangible progress.
The original “early harvest” concept has traditionally been championed by Beijing. Centred historically on less contentious zones like the Sikkim sector, an “early harvest” implies securing low-hanging fruit to build diplomatic momentum while bypassing deeply entrenched disputes.

India has historically viewed this approach with scepticism, fearing it allows China to project a veneer of normalisation while indefinitely postponing resolution in critical strategic zones like Depsang and Demchok in eastern Ladakh. The word ‘substantial’, in this context, does heavy lifting.
In addition, it was announced that “the next meeting of the India-China Expert-Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers [would be held] in September” and that the two sides would “maintain communication on issues including hydrological data sharing, and renewal of the relevant MoUs”. India had long been pushing for communication on sharing hydrological data, the importance of which has been painfully underlined by the catastrophic transboundary flash floods in Nepal and Tibet.

There were also announcements on establishing two additional meeting points for the general-level mechanism/senior highest military commander meetings and opening two new hotlines in the eastern and middle sectors.
Both sides agreed “that any situation on the ground would be addressed promptly through existing diplomatic and military channels, including the WMCC, local commander-level meetings and other agreed mechanisms, to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation along the LAC”.
Since differing perceptions of the LAC give rise to persistent friction, the two sides “discussed ways to improve understanding of LAC in appropriate areas, for better border management”.

Beyond the semantics of delimitation, the eight-point document institutes pragmatic guardrails designed to prevent the skirmishes of the past from cascading into systemic crises. The agreement to establish two additional meeting points for military leadership, alongside two new channels for hotlines, underscores a shared recognition of the frontier’s volatility. Coupled with agreements to reopen designated border trading points and resume hydrological data sharing, these measures represent an effort to stabilise the periphery.

However, while the outcomes provide a framework for diplomatic engagement ahead of the anticipated Xi-Modi summit, their structural significance must not be overstated. These incremental steps are not indications of a radical shift in bilateral ties or green shoots of mutual trust, but rather an effort to put a floor under the relationship.

The dynamic remains fundamentally competitive. The foundational drivers of Sino-Indian tension — structural asymmetries in national composite power, overlapping spheres of influence in the Indian subcontinent and the Indian Ocean Region, China’s tactical patronage of Pakistan and territorial aggrandisement — remain unmitigated.

The eight-point consensus is an instrument of crisis containment, designed to arrest the downward spiral of relations rather than initiate a strategic realignment.
Finally, while the latest outcomes may help in keeping the peace, it is not clear how both sides intend to take up the tricky task of border delimitation.

The operationalisation of an “early and substantial harvest” faces formidable cartographic and strategic hurdles. Converting broad political declarations into mutually acceptable demarcations on high-altitude, militarised terrain, where every ridge line and valley holds tactical value, has eluded negotiators for decades. The creation of buffer zones and the suspension of traditional patrolling rights in sensitive areas remain contentious issues in India, while China shows no inclination to dismantle its aggressive forward infrastructure and force posture.

The Doval-Wang meeting did indicate, however, that both sides are keen to continue with this process of re-engagement. In an increasingly fragmented international order dominated by protectionist shocks from Washington, India and China have chosen pragmatic management over unrestrained confrontation. That’s a wise choice.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Why has Gen Z ignored Afghanistan’s oppressed women and girls?
editorials.passage:
In the era of aggressive cockroaches, who swarm out at the slightest whiff of supposed derisive nouns — the latest being “Dimaagi Naxal” — the Taliban regime’s ongoing oppression of Afghan women does not even provoke a protesting mosquito. It has been five years since night fell on the female sex in Afghanistan as the US troops messily withdrew from there. Since then, the ‘liberal’ world has ignored the almost-casually brutal suppression of women and girls there.

Every year around August 15 — the very day that India celebrates the anniversary of its independence from Britain — stories surface about their plight. But there is no sense of injustice or urgency; no murmur of disgust and ‘rage’ among the ever-volatile Gen Z, the current favourite of regime-change conspirators. Does that generation not exist in Afghanistan? After all, many countries in its vicinity have witnessed widespread Gen Z activities, heavily bolstered by Western praise.

If conscientious Indian Gen Z members pulled off the cockroach protests in India on behalf of their young compatriots, why are they not concerned at all about their co-generationists being oppressed by the Taliban? Their silence is deafening—and revealing. Why have there been no marches for freedom of expression, much less the right to education and even life? Constantly connected Gen Z surely cannot be unaware of what has been happening in Afghanistan under the Taliban?

The curious silence of Gen Z is matched only by the sheer absence of western “humanitarian” lobbying by the usual suspects. Those whose voices cry out for the beleaguered women and girls in Gaza are silent about the ones suffering in Kabul, Jalalabad, Qandahar, Herat and countless other places. What makes Afghanistan a no-go area for any western bleeding-heart activity? The humiliating and ignominious withdrawal of the west from there is only partly to blame.

It seems the much-reviled political system called “democracy” is the prerequisite for getting Gen Z activated. Where the going gets tough—authoritarian Islamist regimes and Communist China—they stay quiet. At least Gen X tried, way back in 1989, to raise the banner of protest in China, now mostly known by the location of their efforts: Tiananmen Square. But while many nations in China’s vicinity have had Gen Z protests, the Communist bastion remains strangely immune.

As for Islamist regimes, Afghanistan’s women and girls have been eclipsed in the limited western mind space by the more pressing wars in the Gulf and Ukraine. As long as those women and girls are tormented behind closed doors, the world (including Gen Z) prefers to forget their existence. The Taliban have also cleverly avoided any acts that may turn the international spotlight back on them, such as publicly executing women “guilty” of violating oppressive Sharia law tenets.
Instead, the Taliban are wearing down Afghanistan’s women and girls mentally and physically by limiting their ability to learn, work and move about. They figure that in a few decades there will be no females left with the mental or physical wherewithal to oppose Islamist oppression. Iran’s ayatollahs’ brutal suppression of the 2025-26 protests that had a Gen Z component underlined that the west failed to follow through on their initial support. That has encouraged the Taliban.

Indeed, it’s been a win-win for the Taliban. Supposed “international isolation” has also worked in their favour. If foreign governments do not officially recognise the Taliban government of Afghanistan, there are no official channels to exert pressure. And foreign nations are also wary of engaging with the Taliban lest that is spun as a legitimisation of their regime. And the Taliban feels they can wear down the west too, which has no stomach for any more war and hostilities.

Some “international” women’s groups — and sundry tax-free salaried UN organisations are “speaking out” but is it likely that the Taliban are paying the slightest heed to them? No. Instead, in the past five years, the Taliban have issued decree after decree further curtailing the human rights of women and girls since capturing Afghanistan. But there are bizarrely favourable media campaigns to aver that those women are “turning” to “entrepreneurship” instead. Really?

Can women who are denied education above primary level (college is absolutely forbidden) and prevented from jobs in most professions including medicine, banking, the judiciary, etc — and forbidden to move outside their homes without male companions ever be “entrepreneurs”? Taliban have literally bound and gagged them, but western media is busy talking about the supposed troubles and “suppression” of freedom of speech in India! Why? Amnesia? Ego? Guilt?

Yet this den of medieval oppression has a huge Gen Z population — 32.2 per cent of Afghans are aged between 14 and 29, the second largest after Gen Alpha at 40.3 per cent. Most of the latter are too young for the political arena but Gen Z has a lot to answer for there. There are 13 million Gen Zs in Afghanistan, with women making up a little less than half that number. But many Gen Z males are obviously Taliban, as they are of fighting age. Are ‘liberal’ Gen Zs elsewhere even aware of this?

Afghanistan’s battle-hardened and deeply regressive Taliban senior leadership may be from Gen X — between 46 and 60 years — but at about 3.4 million they are just about a quarter of the number of Gen Zs. Even if Gen X are in cahoots with Millennials (30 to 45 years, 6 million) they still number far less than Gen Zs. Yet are they being allowed to call the shots while Gen Zs even in next-door nations are not urging their powerful backers to help Afghanistan’s tormented women.

There is perhaps an insidious reason for the strange silence of Afghanistan’s Gen Z on the suppression of their women’s rights. Re-culturation. Historically the area now known as Afghanistan was well within the cultural sphere of Bharat; over the centuries however, after the Islamic conquest and the allied strengthening of rustic tribal mores, Afghan society has lurched into a more conservative mould. The limited media access under the Taliban has been changing attitudes.

Hindi movies and their accompanying social and cultural messages influenced young Afghans for over 60 years. But the Taliban banned all Indian movies and media from there. Instead, the current youth there — Gen Z and Gen Alpha — are being exposed only to Arab, Turkish and Iranian TV shows and movies, whose storylines, clothes, etc, are supposedly “more in line” with Afghan “tradition”. And they already seem to think that Afghan women and girls are not oppressed!

(The author is a freelance writer. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely that of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Bill Gates’ AI warning: India must act before disruption begins
editorials.passage:
In a widely discussed essay published on August 26, 2026, Bill Gates warns that the world is entering “one of the most turbulent times in human history” as artificial intelligence reshapes work, education, security and human relationships — with no coherent plan to manage the transition. For India, this diagnosis is both a call to action and a caution: the same forces that could make AI “the greatest equaliser ever invented” also risk making it “the worst source of injustice”, depending on policy choices made now.

Gates’s nearly 6,000-word essay, titled ‘The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical’, argues that AI is already crossing danger thresholds that the industry itself once said should trigger a pause: mass job displacement, powerful cyber and biological capabilities, emotional dependence on machines, and erosion of human control. He identifies three principal risks.

AI will substitute for human cognition in law, medicine, customer service, software and manufacturing, hitting entry- and mid-level roles hardest and potentially creating structural unemployment that does not self-correct. AI-enabled fraud, deepfakes, cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, and even biotech misuse will scale faster than defensive capacities. AI companions and over-reliance on AI tutors could stunt emotional and cognitive development and replace human relationships, especially for young people. Alongside these risks, Gates stresses AI’s transformative potential in healthcare, education, agriculture, mental health access and government service delivery — areas where India already faces acute capacity constraints.

India’s opportunity lies in leveraging AI to compress decades of development into years, particularly in sectors where the scarcity of skilled professionals is a binding constraint. Gates notes that AI diagnostic tools are already deployed in nearly 2,000 US hospitals; similar systems could extend specialist-level triage to India’s primary health centres, reducing mortality from treatable conditions and easing the burden on overworked doctors. For a country with a low doctor-to-population ratio and vast rural-urban disparities, AI-assisted screening for TB, diabetic retinopathy, cervical cancer and maternal risk could be transformative.

AI tutors that preserve “productive struggle” rather than simply supplying answers could help India address learning deficits revealed by national assessments, while also enabling personalised upskilling for a young workforce facing rapid technological change. In a system where teacher shortages and large class sizes are endemic, AI can act as a force multiplier — if designed to augment, not replace, human instruction.

Gates highlights AI’s potential to give small farmers in low-income countries access to advice on weather, seeds, soil and pests that currently only wealthier farmers receive. For India’s millions of small and marginal farmers, such tools could improve yields, reduce input waste and enhance climate resilience, directly supporting food security and rural incomes.

AI can streamline enrolment and verification for health insurance, food subsidies and welfare schemes, reducing leakage and exclusion errors that have long plagued India’s social protection architecture. Given India’s existing digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker), AI could further lower transaction costs and improve last-mile delivery.

In each of these domains, AI functions as a development accelerant, allowing India to do more with existing fiscal and human resources. Yet Gates’s warnings map uncomfortably well onto India’s structural realities. India’s demographic dividend depends on absorbing millions of young jobseekers annually into formal employment. If AI erodes entry-level roles in IT services, back-office operations, customer support, basic coding, paralegal work and radiology, the “first rung” of the career ladder could vanish before many climb it. Unlike cyclical downturns, this displacement may not reverse with growth, risking a generation of underemployed graduates. With a large informal sector and limited unemployment insurance, India lacks the automatic stabilisers Gates implicitly assumes.

Structural AI-driven job loss could translate quickly into household distress, social unrest and political pressure for short-term fixes rather than strategic adaptation. India’s experience with deepfakes, coordinated disinformation and financial fraud suggests AI will amplify existing vulnerabilities. Criminals with limited skills could target individuals, firms and even government systems at unprecedented scale, as Gates warns. In an electoral democracy with intense information warfare, AI-generated content could further erode trust in institutions. With high smartphone penetration and heavy social media use among Indian youth, AI companions and hyper-personalised content risk deepening isolation, anxiety and attention fragmentation. In a context where mental health services are scarce, technology-induced harms could outpace the capacity to respond.

Gates’s central claim is that the outcome is not technologically determined but politically chosen: AI will be an equaliser or an engine of injustice depending on governance. For India, this implies several priorities. Gates proposes a “Human Reserved” category of jobs closed to machines, potentially up to 40 per cent of roles, to preserve human-to-human interaction in care, education and public services. India could adapt this by mandating human presence in frontline health, schooling, policing and welfare delivery, using AI as backend support rather than front-end replacement. Gates suggests taxing AI tokens or robots akin to payroll taxes to fund retraining and social protection. India could explore levies on high-value AI deployments or data-intensive platforms, channelling revenues into lifelong learning, vocational transitions and regional development in AI-exposed sectors.

Gates calls for new national bodies and international institutions to coordinate AI policy, given the cross-border nature of the risks. India’s existing AI mission and sectoral regulators could be strengthened into a coherent architecture that balances innovation with safeguards, while engaging in global norm-setting to avoid a race to the bottom.

Policies could limit AI companions in schools, require transparency in AI tutoring systems, and invest in human-centric pedagogy that uses AI to enhance, not substitute for, teacher-student interaction. Gates’s essay is a mirror for India’s AI moment: it shows both the scale of opportunity and the depth of danger. If India treats AI as a strategic public good — embedding it in health, education, agriculture and governance while protecting human roles and relationships — it can harness the technology to narrow inequalities and accelerate development.

If, however, it allows market forces alone to dictate adoption, AI could entrench existing disparities, displace the very youth who are supposed to drive growth, and amplify misinformation and insecurity. The difference between these futures will be determined not by the technology itself, but by the clarity and courage of India’s policy choices in the next few years.

(Hindol Sengupta is Professor of International Relations at O. P. Jindal Global University. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely that of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Beyond the sky: Why India needs a unified space command for the wars of tomorrow
editorials.passage:
India faces a critical turning point in its space programme, confronted with a profound strategic contradiction requiring urgent government intervention and far-reaching institutional restructuring. Although India has achieved remarkable technological successes — including the triumphant Mission Shakti anti-satellite demonstration in 2019 and the advanced Project NETRA space surveillance capabilities — the nation remains bound by an anachronistic institutional framework that regards space operations as scientific pursuits rather than instruments of national strategic power.

This dangerous disconnect between India’s technological prowess and its strategic approach undermines national security at precisely the moment when rival powers have discarded fragmented space structures in favour of unified, integrated command systems. The opportunity for India to correct this fundamental institutional deficiency grows narrower with each passing month, and failure to act may create strategic disadvantages lasting for generations.

This paradox originates from a single geographic marker positioned 100 km above Earth. Historically, the Kármán Line functioned merely as a scientific reference point differentiating where conventional aircraft operations conclude and space operations commence. Its creators never envisioned it serving as an operational boundary, administrative dividing line or strategic demarcation. Nevertheless, Indian military thinking has transformed this arbitrary altitude threshold into an institutional barrier rigidly separating military command responsibilities and strategic authority.

The Indian Air Force maintains exclusive operational control beneath this imaginary line, commanding all conventional military assets. Above it, civilian-administered space organisations function according to mandates emphasising scientific research over military applications. While this institutional separation may appear administratively convenient, it can limit strategic integration and has gradually become embedded in established doctrine, potentially creating challenges for India’s evolving national security requirements.

Evidence overwhelmingly demonstrates that India’s space approach suffers from a profound organisational deficiency with significant national security consequences. By rigidly formalising the Kármán Line into military doctrine, India has created a strategic obstacle masquerading as operational necessity. This institutional architecture has spawned organisational compartmentalisation that fragments India’s space capabilities precisely when competitors have already achieved seamless integration across all space domains. This fragmentation constitutes a fundamental strategic weakness that rival powers have identified and systematically exploited through their own comprehensive institutional realignment.

Comparing India’s space structure with competitor nations reveals starkly divergent approaches and concerning implications. America established an independent space force operating as a military service equal to traditional branches, positioning space as the primary operational environment for future conflicts. China executed an even more transformative institutional reorganisation in April 2024. Beijing consolidated space, information warfare and cyber operations into the autonomous PLA Aerospace Force, achieving unified command authority over every Chinese spaceport and launch vehicle.

This strategic restructuring eliminates the artificial compartmentalisation constraining Indian operations; China now manages space as an integrated strategic domain operating under singular command oversight. Russia’s consolidated Aerospace Forces structure demonstrates a similar integrated philosophy, treating atmospheric and space operations as interconnected components of unified operational theatres rather than separate military domains.

These leading powers understand space as the fundamental strategic environment determining military dominance throughout this century. Conversely, India persists in employing fragmented institutional arrangements that undermine strategic integration. This reflects the absence of a comprehensive strategic vision and serious government dedication to treating space as a fundamental national security priority.

Government leaders must recognise that India’s notable space accomplishments, though technically credible, remain fundamentally protective and reactive rather than strategically offensive. The Mission Shakti demonstration proved India’s capacity to eliminate orbital targets but established no persistent operational doctrine. Project NETRA delivers advanced space observation capabilities, yet observation capability alone cannot generate strategic superiority. GSAT communications satellites provide dependable services but require comprehensive logistical networks for sustainable operation. Near-space doctrine concentrates on hypersonic countermeasures but ignores cislunar domains where competitors increasingly consolidate power.

The Indian Navy’s extraordinary metamorphosis from a coastal defence force to a genuine maritime superpower offers essential strategic instruction that space planners have regrettably neglected. This naval transformation emerged not from technological advancement alone but from a fundamental reconceptualisation of operational geography. The Navy comprehended the maritime environment as a comprehensive operational space extending from the surface to ocean depths.

Naval leadership never artificially subdivided this domain at random depth measurements or assigned competing authorities to surface versus submarine operations. Rather, the Navy acknowledged that commanding the totality of maritime space — treating the entire water column as a singular integrated domain — established overwhelming naval superiority. Space strategy requires an identical philosophical orientation.

An aerospace force conceptualising the complete atmosphere-space-cislunar spectrum as a unified strategic domain will necessarily dominate forces restricted to Earth’s immediate vicinity. This represents fundamental military logic, not theoretical abstraction, already operationalised globally by competitors. Contemporary military science demonstrates the inseparable linkage between atmospheric and space operations. Detection systems depend fundamentally on orbital platforms.
Telecommunications infrastructure blends ground and orbital components. Intelligence operations span both atmospheric and orbital dimensions. Separating these operationally connected capabilities under fragmented authorities creates strategic dysfunction that undermines military effectiveness.

India’s strategic window for establishing itself as a space-capable power is contracting dangerously. China declared Moon-landing aspirations before 2030 subsequent to Chang’e-6’s 2024 far-side sample retrieval, representing concrete near-term military objectives directing resource distribution and technological advancement. Additionally, Sino-Russian cooperation on an International Lunar Research Station, with construction set to begin imminently, produces cislunar competencies neither nation could individually establish. America’s Artemis initiative incorporates military infrastructure throughout cislunar domains, supporting roughly ten operational spacecraft.

Effective space capabilities necessitate six interconnected competencies: deploying assets cislunar-ward, executing hostile operations, manoeuvring through orbital pathways, providing logistical sustainment, defending against threats and recovering personnel safely. These represent doctrinal imperatives, not hardware prerequisites. Military institutions require restructuring immediately.

India must urgently establish a robust space command, reform military doctrine beyond the limitations of the Kármán Line, create specialised space education and coordinate the development of critical orbital infrastructure. ISRO, DRDO and IN-SPACe should operate under an integrated strategic framework. Space must be recognised as a core operational domain, with India’s future space power depending on immediate strategic commitment, institutional integration and decisive national will as a matter of national security.

(Dr Nishakant Ojha specialises in Aerospace Security, Artificial Intelligence and Next-Generation Defence Technologies, providing strategic advisory services across multiple nations. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely that of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Nepal-Tibet Flash Floods, Kailash Pilgrimage, and the Question of Fate
editorials.passage: Sixteen years ago, almost to the day, I travelled the same Himalayan road that hundreds of Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrims travelled this week. I crossed the Friendship Bridge that no longer exists. Today the Bhote Koshi river has reclaimed it—and hundreds of lives besides.Before sunrise, amid a rousing chorus of “Har Har Mahadev!” (Victory to the Supreme Lord Shiva), our tarnished bus chugged out of a Kathmandu hotel, belching diesel fumes into the drizzle. It carried far more than 16 pilgrims. Stuffed inside and lashed precariously onto the roof were two weeks' rations, gas cylinders, sleeping bags, duffel bags, a cook, three Sherpas, a Sherpa sardar, and the collective faith of people who believed they were travelling to the holiest mountain on earth. It was mid-September—and the monsoon had overstayed its welcome. For two anxious weeks I had watched satellite images of Nepal and southern Tibet, hoping for a break in the weather. The cloud cover refused to lift.Only if we could cross the high Lalung La Pass into the rain shadow of the Trans-Himalaya would we finally escape the tyranny of the monsoon. Nepal’s Flash Floods Show the Devastating Power of ‘Cascading Hazards’The night before departure, Kathmandu had drowned beneath sheets of rain. By dawn, however, fierce winds were tearing the clouds apart. The Rain Gods have always treated me kindly—but they offered no such assurances about the road. The road through the valley of the Bhote River had been given a sound hammering by the seasonal rains and was in a dreadful condition. Massive landslides and huge boulders had hurtled down the mountainsides and blocked our path. Whenever a slushy landslide had to be crossed, I jumped off the bus on the pretext of taking a picture and walked across it, having more faith in my trembling legs than the balding tyres of the bus that rocked, groaned, skid, and slid across the mire.  At one bend the outer edge of the dirt track had been washed away completely. On my side of the bus the valley disappeared vertically into the roaring river thousands of feet below.As we lurched forward, one of the rear tyres hung briefly in empty space. Before I could say my last prayer, we were on safe ground. I never fail to admire the courage of the fate-tempting, foolhardy bus and truck drivers of the Himalaya.   The Bhote Koshi accompanied us all day. It was not a river in the comforting sense of the word. It did not meander or sparkle. It exploded.Fed by glaciers and monsoon rains, it hurled itself through the gorge with a violence that made conversation inside the bus impossible. Sometimes it vanished beneath cliffs, only for its thunder to rise through the valley like artillery. At other times it appeared beside us, white with rage, smashing itself against black boulders. By late afternoon we reached Kodari.17 Dead in Nepal-Tibet Border Flash Flood, Villages Washed AwayThe border town was unrecognisable. Years earlier, in 1994, while returning from the Central Asia Expedition, I had crossed into Nepal through what had then been little more than a sleepy frontier post with a handful of houses. Growing trade with China had transformed Kodari into a bustling, chaotic settlement where endless lines of trucks clogged the narrow streets and warehouses competed with shabby hotels for every available inch of land. While we exchanged Indian rupees for Chinese yuan over lunch, frail women porters—wrinkled beyond their years—unloaded our baggage from the bus. Bent almost double beneath impossible loads, they carried our worldly possessions towards the bridge while we followed with cameras around our necks and pilgrimage on our lips. Then we walked across the Friendship Bridge. Halfway across, a young, sullen Chinese soldier, motionless as a statue, stood at attention, gun in hand. I felt like tickling him, but his bayonet was too sharp.  Outside the immigration hall we were joined by a Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrimage group from Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu. Around us swarmed Tibetan porters carrying enormous sacks from which protruded sheep's hooves.  Mash, a Texas-educated, notoriously worldly Sindhi spinster in her mid-30s, working as a psychological counsellor, a clairvoyant, a regression analyst and a spiritual tour leader, affected by the swarming legions of poor, scrawny porters in patched shoes and tattered rags, asked me what I thought of “all this poverty”.   “Fate,” I replied. She looked at me sharply. “What do you mean?” I told her an old conversation between Shiva and Parvati. One day, Parvati looked upon the world and challenged Shiva. “How can you call yourself the Supreme Lord,” she asked, “when there is so much hunger, disease, and misery?” “They are fated to suffer,” Shiva replied. “Hogwash,” said Parvati. Shiva smiled. A beggar was walking along a forest path. Shiva sliced open a watermelon, filled it with gold coins, sealed it perfectly and placed it in the beggar's way. The beggar picked up the watermelon, took it to a grocer and exchanged it for 14 pieces of bread. “You see?” Shiva said. “Had he cut the fruit, he would have discovered the treasure. But it was not his fate.” “Rubbish,” Parvati protested. “How was he to know? Bread is more precious to a hungry man than fruit.” “Then watch again,” Shiva replied. This time he split a melon in half, stuffed it with gold coins and left it open on the path, the treasure glistening in plain sight. As the beggar approached, an odd curiosity struck him. “I wonder,” he thought, “what it feels like to be blind.” He closed his eyes—and walked straight past the fortune that could have transformed his life. “Now do you believe me?” Shiva asked. Before Mash could demolish my philosophy, the Tibetan guide shepherded us into the immigration hall, where surprisingly cheerful young Chinese officials stamped our passports and welcomed us into Tibet. Beyond the border, five Toyota Land Cruisers carried us towards Nyalam through the gorge of the Matsang Tsangpo, as Bhote Koshi is known in Tibet. The rain returned with astonishing ferocity. Waterfalls poured from every mountain. The river disappeared beneath clouds but never ceased roaring.Nepalese traders had long called Nyalam the ‘Gate to Hell’, for the old dirt track climbing from the border had been one of the most terrifying roads in the Himalaya. I had driven it once before on a thunderous night. Rain had poured down in amazing volumes. Ear-splitting lightning crackled as diligently as the deafening thunder. Loose rocks, pushed by the furious winds, assaulted the vehicle’s roof and bonnet. I had reached the relative safety of Zhangmu with shivering bones—but delighted at having come out of the storm in one piece.  The Chinese later replaced that perilous dirt track with an immaculate highway, reinforced with tunnels, retaining walls and engineering that bordered on the miraculous. Sitting comfortably inside our vehicles, we admired waterfalls drifting sideways in the wind and forests dissolving into mist.Explained: Why Western Nepal Is More Prone to Earthquakes It was tempting to believe that human ingenuity had finally conquered the mountains. But the Himalaya have a cruel habit of correcting such arrogance. This week the Bhote Koshi reminded us who truly owns the valley. The Friendship Bridge has vanished. Kodari village and roads have been torn apart. Hundreds of pilgrims who set out chanting “Har Har Mahadev” have simply disappeared into the river's fury. And ever since I heard the news, I have found myself returning to that conversation between Shiva and Parvati. Were those pilgrims destined to die? If destiny had written their names beside that river long before they boarded their buses, what are we to make of the families who persuaded them to go? Of the drivers who chose to leave an hour earlier or later? Of the traveller who stopped to buy tea and therefore missed the flood by five minutes? And if their deaths were not fated, how do we explain the terrifying lottery by which one pilgrim survives while another, walking a few steps ahead, is swept away forever? Faith offers one vocabulary. Science offers another. The mountains remain indifferent to both. Perhaps Parvati was right all along. Perhaps the beggar did not miss the gold because destiny condemned him to poverty. Perhaps he missed it because human lives are woven from countless ordinary choices, coincidences and moments that only acquire meaning after tragedy. Or perhaps Shiva was right—that there exists a design too vast for our frightened minds to comprehend. I do not know. What I do know is this. Sixteen years ago, almost to the day, I crossed that bridge with laughter in my heart, irreverent jokes on my lips, and the excitement of approaching Kailash. I remember the old women carrying our luggage, the impassive soldier, the thunder of the Bhote Koshi beneath my feet, and a philosophical argument about fate that seemed little more than an entertaining diversion while waiting for immigration clearance. Today the bridge, immigration hall and parts of Kodari exist only in memory. The river still roars through the gorge, as eternal as the Himalaya themselves. The pilgrims who travelled that road were seeking Shiva on Mount Kailash. Whether they found their destiny, their God, or merely the terrible unpredictability of nature is a question that neither philosophy nor pilgrimage can answer. Perhaps only the mountains and tectonic plates know. (Akhil Bakshi is the author of Stairway to Heaven: Circumambulation of Mt. Kailash in Tibet.)
